<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 31 Oct 2026 02:38:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Talks between unions and Government over new pay deal finish without agreement]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/31/talks-between-unions-and-government-over-new-pay-deal-finish-without-agreement/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/31/talks-between-unions-and-government-over-new-pay-deal-finish-without-agreement/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 00:24:08 +0000The prospect of a second national public service strike grew on Friday evening as talks between Government representatives and union leaders at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) concluded without agreement.

Speaking as the talks ended at about 11.30pm, Kevin Callinan, general secretary of Fórsa, said it had become clear that the gap between the two sides was too great to close at this stage and, with no further talks planned for over the weekend, he and the other trade union participants in the process would now brief the other public service unions on Monday.

“It doesn’t seem possible at this moment that we’re going to be able to reach an agreement that we could confidently put to our members in a ballot so our next step is to meet with our affiliate unions on Monday morning, where we’ll brief them on the negotiations, and decide on what comes next,” he said.

Asked if it was possible the two sides would be brought back together under the auspices of the Kevin Foley-led committee appointed to help resolve the outstanding difficulties that had originally prevented the talks getting started, Callinan said that was a matter for the WRC but that the unions would remain available and would attend any process initiated.

“But we really need to be confident that any proposals would be likely to be accepted by members of the ballot, and we’re a long way from that,” he said.

He said the union side had been consistent from the outset with regard to the issues that needed to be addressed by Government in terms of the gap between pay increases and inflation over the past five years, an increase for the second half of this year and measures to ensure members were protected against spikes in inflation over the course of any new deal and agreement.

A second national public services strike will be scheduled for Wednesday, November 11th, if no deal between the Government and trade unions on a new pay agreement is reached over the weekend, Callinan said earlier.

Callinan, who is also chair of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions’ public services committee, said the 19 unions it encompasses should meet on Monday to get an update on the talks and, if no agreement has been reached by then, to discuss taking further action.

He said the strike, which would again close the State’s schools and severely affect health, local authority and other services, would allow for demonstrations in Dublin and other big urban centres by more than 300,000 staff affected.

In an earlier update to the 100,000 members of his own union, Callinan said the talks had been “lengthy and at times heated” and that while a deal remains possible “the Government has yet to put forward a credible offer, and it remains to be seen whether it will do so”.

He said it remains unclear whether an agreement can be reached over the coming days.

Referencing the prospect of another one-day stoppage, Callinan told members: “If we fail to reach an acceptable agreement by the weekend, it leaves unions with no alternative but to escalate the action.”

Senior officials from the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform as well as the four union leaders participating in the main negotiations arrived for the latest session at 10am on Friday.

There had been some optimism that an agreement could be reached if the two sides pushed through the night on Thursday, but in the end it was concluded that their respective conditions were not close enough to continue past about 10pm.

Arrangements for a second national strike on November 11th have to be put in place early next week as seven days’ notice must be given.

In health, the required notice period is generally three weeks but the unions believe they are covered by the original notice of action served last month and the continuing work-to-rule.

The potential for another national stoppage may be viewed by the Government side as an attempt by the unions to leverage their power as the talks enter what one source described as their “crunch period”.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Heavyweight tech stocks plummet as AI cash burn spooks investors]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/30/heavyweight-tech-stocks-plummet-as-ai-cash-burn-spooks-investors/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/30/heavyweight-tech-stocks-plummet-as-ai-cash-burn-spooks-investors/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 18:47:09 +0000European ‌shares dropped on Friday, hammered by a global tech sell-off that shaved billions of dollars off the market values of some chip heavyweights, ending ​a largely strong month on a sour note.

Results from Amazon and Intel in the US rekindled concerns about the high costs of building out artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and ​it prompted a pullback from technology names worldwide.

Dublin

The Irish index ended Friday on a low note, losing just under 1 per cent over the day as banking shares and construction stocks dragged the market lower.

But the Euronext Dublin closed the week up 1.1 per cent.

AIB lost 2.2 per cent on Friday, while Bank of Ireland was down 2.6 per cent, mirroring weakness seen in financial stocks in other European markets.

Construction stocks also had a poor showing, with insulation specialist Kingspan down 1.7 per cent and home builders Glenveagh and Cairn also off the pace.

Ryanair ended the week at €22.90, a 0.3 per cent decline on the day but a 0.4 per cent gain over the week.

Food group Kerry put on 1.9 per cent, while Glanbia was 2.9 per cent higher on the day.

London

The ​blue-chip FTSE 100 index ended about 0.1 per cent higher at 10,729.78 points, rising over 1 per cent in October. The midcap FTSE 250 slipped nearly 1 per cent on the day.

AstraZeneca jumped 7 per cent in its best day in a year after the ⁠Anglo-Swedish drugmaker announced a restructuring drive.

​Banks weighed most on the ​index on Friday after NatWest lost nearly 9 per cent following a weaker-than-expected outlook for ‌interest income.

Precious and industrial metal ​miners lost 5.3 per cent and 2.9 per cent, respectively, tracking declines in gold and ⁠copper.

BP rose 0.5 per cent ⁠after posting ​a record quarterly net profit.

Consumer staples stocks rose on the day, with British American Tobacco and Unilever up 1.7 per cent and 2.1 per cent respectively.

Europe

The pan-European STOXX 600 index closed 0.36 per cent lower at 646.75 points, despite recording its best month since June.

The European technology sector index fell 2.75 per cent for its ‌worst ‌day ​since July 7th and led sectoral declines. AT&S, Soitec and Technoprobe led losses on the Stoxx 600, with declines ranging from 9 per cent to 13 per cent.

Universal Music ‌Group jumped 7.89 per cent, topping the Stoxx ⁠600, after posting a pickup in subscription streaming revenue in the third quarter.

BP rose marginally after posting third-quarter net income ahead of expectations, while German sportswear ‌maker Puma advanced 5.59 per cent after a quarterly sales beat.

Sanofi gained 4.71 per cent after the French pharmaceutical firm reported third-quarter results ahead of analyst expectations ​and lifted its outlook.

Among other movers, Bayer gained 5.46 per cent after winning a ​trial on Thursday over claims by three women that its Roundup weedkiller caused their cancer.

New York

By the close of trading in Europe, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index had fallen 3.5 per cent, on track for its worst month since March 2025, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.8 per cent.

Amazon shares slumped 2.1 per cent, as the company’s AI spending plans and lagging ecommerce business overshadowed solid growth in cloud sales in the eyes of investors after it reported earnings on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Intel was eyeing its worst one-day drop on record after the chipmaker reported a revenue forecast that missed analysts’ estimates, hurt by sputtering demand for PC processors and supply-chain problems with its lucrative data-centre components. Shares fell 30 per cent.

Intel’s rivals Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia were down 12 per cent and 4.6 per cent respectively.

Outside of tech, ExxonMobil Holdings reported earnings before the bell on Friday that surpassed expectations on the strength of surging gasoline and diesel prices that pushed refining results to an all-time high. The shares gained 1.8 per cent. Chevron also beat expectations, sending shares up 1.6 per cent. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]>Sarah Yenesel<![CDATA[Supreme Court refuses appeal against Co Carlow wind turbines]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/2026/10/30/supreme-court-refuses-appeal-against-co-carlow-wind-turbines/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/2026/10/30/supreme-court-refuses-appeal-against-co-carlow-wind-turbines/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:43:50 +0000The Supreme Court has refused to grant an appeal by two residents and an environmental group against the approval of planning permission for the construction of seven wind turbines in Co Carlow.

Last May, the High Court dismissed a challenge to the grant of planning permission given by An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to EDF Renewables Ireland Ltd for the turbines in an area of Carlow known as Killeshin Hills, Ridge, Agharue, Coonnakishna and Seskinrea.

The challenge had been brought by information technology professional Stephen Keogh, who lives a few kilometres from the proposed development, and by farmer Tom Quirke, who lives less than a kilometre from the site. A non-governmental organisation called the Rural Residents Wind Aware and Environmental Group also brought the challenge.

Following its decision, the challengers then asked the High Court for leave to appeal its decision to the Court of Appeal, but this was refused.

The challengers then sought a direct appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds that the case raised matters of public importance or was in the interests of justice. ACP opposed granting leave to appeal while EDF was a notice party.

A central point of the challengers’ argument was the application of the Government’s 2006 rules for wind farm developments, the Wind Energy Development Guidelines. These are not binding but are matters to which ACP is required to have regard in making its decisions.

The Supreme Court said the objectors had essentially maintained that the separation distances between the seven turbines did not comply with requirements of the guidelines. This provides that any proposed layout of wind turbines takes into account the development potential of an adjoining site for a similar development.

The Supreme Court said the High Court, in its decision, had not misapplied the guidelines.

In a written determination, the Supreme Court refused to grant an appeal.

The court did not consider that the application for an appeal met the constitutional criteria of public importance and interests of justice.

It said it should be observed that the ACP inspector and ACP itself were only “to have regard” to the guidelines, “which they clearly did”.

]]>Narumon Bowonkitwanchai<![CDATA[‘No evidence’ Bawag’s €1.6bn PTSB offer is ‘bad deal for shareholders’, court told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/no-evidence-bawags-16bn-ptsb-offer-is-bad-deal-for-shareholders-court-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/no-evidence-bawags-16bn-ptsb-offer-is-bad-deal-for-shareholders-court-told/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:01:10 +0000There is “simply no evidence” that the €1.6 billion proposal from Austrian lender Bawag to acquire PTSB for €2.97 a share “is a bad deal for shareholders”, the High Court has heard, while it remains the “only price on offer” despite “musings and mutterings” otherwise.

There is “not a jot of evidence to suggest the Minister [for Finance] was motivated by anything other than price” when he voted in favour of the bid, which would see the end of the State’s ownership of Ireland’s third largest bank, Lyndon MacCann, counsel for the Minister, told Judge Michael Quinn on Friday.

Then minister for finance Brian Lenihan jnr, when buying 99.2 per cent of PTSB in 2011, did so “not for some opportunistic commercial venture”, but “to come to the aid of a flailing bank during a time of financial crisis”, MacCann told the court.

The proposed takeover of PTSB by Bawag, which is subject to High Court approval, has been before the court this week. Proceedings were dominated by objections to the deal from four minority shareholders who, collectively, own 0.00287 per cent of the bank.

They allege the acquisition should not be sanctioned as, among other reasons, the Minister benefits from “special, incredible” rights not enjoyed by other shareholders, which led to unequal access to information during the bid’s consultation process.

However, to argue this point “involved turning logic on its head”, MacCann said.

Piotr Skocylas, a litigating shareholder who has addressed the court for the past four days, briefly questioned the constitutionality of the Minister’s holding of PTSB shares on Thursday. He has repeatedly lamented the way in which he acquired his current 57.5 per cent stake.

Shareholders have acquired their stake in the company through various different means, he said, with some buying, inheriting or being given their shares at various different prices.

“Irrespective of how we got here, we got here lawfully,” MacCann said.

He added that Skocylas “has not put any evidence before that court that the scheme is a bad deal for shareholders”.

“All he has put before the court is photocopies of two reports,” he said, citing an S&P newsletter and Business Post article, which quote financial analysts’ opinions on the acquisition offer.

“They are entitled to their view, but this is not evidence that an intelligent or honest member of the class could not have reasonably voted in favour of the scheme,” MacCann said, citing the legal threshold for the scheme to be approved.

The litigating shareholders also claim the Minister was swayed in favour of the bid for commercial and somewhat political reasons, such as Bawag’s assertion that PTSB’s headquarters would remain in Dublin and there would be little to no change in its branch footprint. This, they say, has resulted in the Minister opting for a “derisory” price point.

But MacCann said share price was the “dominant motivator” behind the Minister’s support. “The only price on offer is the price offered by Bawag,” he said. “That is the best price because there is no other price on offer.”

Meanwhile, Axis Capital “is not within a country mile” of preparing a tangible counter offer, MacCann said in court, despite “mutterings and musings” from the advisory firm cofounded by Mark Duffy, the former chief executive of Bank of Scotland Ireland.

Last Thursday the firm said it would seek an adjournment of this week’s High Court proceedings of up to six weeks to allow time for it to prepare a rival bid. The court heard on Wednesday Axis could offer €3.20 per share by way of a bid supported by “one of the most esteemed investment banks in the world”.

Kelley Smith, counsel for PTSB, told the court Axis “lacks the resources to actually implement an offer” and “has no track record of M&A [merger and acquisition] transactions”.

“Axis is a €100 company,” she said, pointing to financial accounts for the year ended May 2026 that “showed €100 on its balance sheet”.

]]><![CDATA[New Government investment accounts could generate up to €400m in fees for banks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/new-investment-accounts-could-generate-up-to-400m-in-fees-for-banks/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/new-investment-accounts-could-generate-up-to-400m-in-fees-for-banks/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:14:08 +0000Personal investment accounts (PIAs) could generate up to €400 million in additional fee income for banks and other providers by 2035, according to Davy Stockbrokers.

The brokerage estimated that, at peak, up to €4 billion in annual investment could flow into these accounts “although the path to this level is uncertain”.

This presented “a potentially meaningful fee opportunity for providers able to capture the flow”, it said.

Greater administrative, tax and reporting requirements in Ireland would favour “scaled providers” such as banks and life assurance companies, Davy said. Online brokers are also expected to offer accounts.

“Applying a range of fee outcomes to our annual flow assumptions implies €100-€400 million of annual fee income by 2035, with the opportunity building as PIA assets accumulate,” it said.

“The onboarding and administrative requirements for PIAs should favour established providers over smaller, more niche providers, resulting in the Irish banks as natural beneficiaries,” Davy said.

Authors Thomas Ryan and Diarmaid Sheridan of Davy said the estimate of cumulative fees was based on an assumption that providers would charge 0.25-1 per cent of the account balance in annual fees.

They said the research was based on a number of assumptions about the number of people who might invest and their likely level of investment, which were based on existing savings and earnings data.

The new State-sponsored investment accounts, launched by Minister for Finance Simon Harris in the budget, will allow individuals to invest up to €12,000 a year in an account.

The accounts, which will be launched in July next year, will have a tax-free threshold of €50,000 after which a flat rate of 1 per cent will be charged.

Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?

The aim is to incentivise Irish savers to move some of the €170 billion held in low-interest-bearing deposit accounts back into capital markets.

Harris has described this money as “sitting idle”.

Davy said the scheme would “allow for a meaningful tax advantage relative to existing investment structures.”

“Our scenario analysis implies an effective tax rate of about 6 per cent over eight years compared with about 30 per cent for comparable investment vehicles,” it said.

The brokerage said the new scheme offered “a compelling economic proposition for investors” while noting international precedent pointed to a gradual adoption, with comparable UK and Swedish schemes having limited impact on existing savings patterns.

“PIAs should provide a welcome tailwind to Irish retail investing,” it said.

“We expect adoption to be gradual with flows captured at the margin from existing alternatives,” it said.

Recently published research from life insurance and pensions company Royal London Ireland looked at how much people believe they would set aside in the proposed PIA.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?

It suggested as many as six in 10 adults in Ireland could invest up to €250 per month in the scheme.

It also indicated that men, on average, expect to invest more than three times as much as women, at €893 per month compared with €240.

Harris first mooted his intention to introduce a new form of consumer-friendly investment account back in February.

His department is understood to have examined similar types of accounts operating in other countries. Ultimately, it opted largely for the Swedish model despite strong industry lobbying in favour of the rival UK individual savings account model.

]]>paparazzit<![CDATA[Lisa McGowan cosmetics business makes €1.39m profit after just two years]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/lisa-mcgowan-cosmetics-business-makes-139m-profit-after-just-two-years/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/lisa-mcgowan-cosmetics-business-makes-139m-profit-after-just-two-years/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:21:05 +0000A cosmetics firm co-owned by Tullamore-based fashion entrepreneur and social media influencer, Lisa McGowan has reported profits of €1.39 million after tax in just its second full year of operation.

That is more than double the €598,453 profits that Jentro Ltd – trading as Lisa & Co Cosmetics – recorded in the prior 14 months.

Underlining the strength of the Lisa McGowan brand in the Irish beauty industry, the company’s accumulated profits had grown to €1.88 million at the end of its financial year in February.

McGowan co-owns the business with beauty entrepreneur Una Tynan on a 50/50 basis. It was only incorporated in 2023.

The Lisa & Co Cosmetics website declares that its goal is to create “a premium range of cosmetics for busy women of all ages that is fuss free and easy to use”.

“Our mission is to empower women to embrace their authentic selves by enhancing their natural beauty. We are Pro Age and Body Positive.”

Highlighting the expansion of the business in 2025, cash funds increased from €117,934 to €467,219 while the value of the company’s stock rose from €158,338 to €1.395 million.

The abridged accounts don’t disclose revenues for the year. The company’s products are available online and are also stocked by Dunnes Stores and in hundreds of pharmacies around the State.

The business is separate to McGowan’s main company, Lisa’s Lust List Ltd, which recorded a profit after tax of €418,268 in 2025.

McGowan’s businesses have flourished in the past number of years. She only started her online promotional work after she won the best-dressed lady competition at the Galway Races in 2016.

McGowan paid herself a package of almost €1.9 million from Lisa’s Lust List – pay of €1.5 million and €384,002 in pension contributions.

That came after a remuneration package of €3 million she received in 2024, comprising €2.67 million in emoluments and €384,002 in pension contributions.

Earlier this month, McGowan put the finances of Lisa’s Lust List beyond public scrutiny,

reregistering Lisa’s Lust List as “Unlimited” where it is no longer required to file annual accounts to the Companies Office.

]]>Andrew Downes, xposure<![CDATA[Nasdaq tumbles at open as Amazon, Intel add to AI spending woes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/30/nasdaq-tumbles-at-open-as-amazon-intel-add-to-ai-spending-woes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/30/nasdaq-tumbles-at-open-as-amazon-intel-add-to-ai-spending-woes/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:46:03 +0000The ‌Nasdaq opened at its ‌lowest level in more than two ​months on Friday, after Amazon’s aggressive artificial intelligence (AI) spending ​plan and Intel’s ⁠cash burn warning intensified ‌investor concerns ‌about ​escalating costs of AI ⁠infrastructure ​buildout and the ​return timeline.

The Dow ‌Jones Industrial Average ​rose 0.08 per cent. The S&P 500 rose 1.16 per cent, while ⁠the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.26 per cent.

Before trading even began, the big names in tech were all plummeting down the index.

Intel ‌tumbled 25 per cent in premarket trading on a bleak outlook, deepening a broader retreat in technology stocks as investors grew increasingly ‌wary of weakening PC demand and the vast spending required to build out AI infrastructure.

The forecast underscores the challenges facing ​chief executive Lip-Bu Tan’s turnaround effort, with Intel still grappling with a prolonged PC market slump even as it invests heavily in AI and manufacturing expansion.

Semiconductor stocks, including Advanced Micro Devices, Arm Holdings, Qualcomm, Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron, fell between 2 per cent and 9 per cent ​in premarket trading.

“The market is in a sell first, ask questions later mood right now, and Intel’s warning has given ⁠investors an easy excuse to take some money off the table across chip stocks,” said Matt ‌Britzman, ‌senior ​equity analyst, Hargreaves Lansdown.

The sell-off spread to server makers, reflecting investor caution towards companies tied to the semiconductor and AI infrastructure supply chain.

Shares of server makers ⁠Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Super ​Micro Computer fell between 6 per cent and 12 per cent in ​pre-market trading. – Reuters

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[Are extended warranties worth the money?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/30/are-extended-warranties-worth-the-money/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/30/are-extended-warranties-worth-the-money/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 12:51:21 +0000You’ve just bought yourself a new washing machine with so many different spin cycles you could choose a different one for every day of the month. Or maybe it’s a fancy new TV, with a 4K display, an AI assistant and a screen that covers half your sittingroom wall.

The shop assistant scans your item and next comes the inevitable question: “Would you like to buy another three years of cover for your new [insert product]?”

The washing machine has just set you back €650 and the TV a cool €1,399. The money you’ve spent should ensure both are still in decent working condition several years later.

But what if something were to go wrong? Perhaps the extra couple of hundred euro for enhanced insurance would be worth the investment?

The nightmare scenario of the washing machine or TV going kaput a week after the warranty expires flashes through your mind.

But what would you really be paying for, and how much better is it than the protection you already have under consumer law?

The first thing to know is you have very robust rights as a consumer in Ireland, and indeed throughout the EU.

If a fault emerges with a product within 30 days of buying or receiving it, you are entitled to cancel your purchase. Under your “short-term right to terminate a sales contract”, you can opt for a repair or, if you prefer, a replacement.

Your legal position is particularly strong during the first year of ownership, but your rights in relation to faulty goods can extend for up to six years if the product – such as a washing machine or TV – could reasonably be expected to last that long.

It is important to note that your contract is with the retailer, not the manufacturer, and it is the retailer’s responsibility to remedy faulty products.

Consumer law does not, however, cover ordinary wear and tear, or products that were misused or accidentally damaged.

Serious problems, if they arise, still have to be dealt with. For the first year, the law is generally on your side and assumes the fault was already there when you bought the product.

After that, the onus shifts to you to show the problem was inherent in the product rather than caused by wear and tear, misuse or accidental damage.

And this is where extended warranties or appliance insurance might begin to offer something extra.

There are, broadly speaking, two types of cover you’re likely to be offered.

Extended warranties usually offer additional repair or replacement cover, sometimes extending beyond the manufacturer’s guarantee.

Insurance policies, on the other hand, offer wider protection and that can include things such as accidental damage. Naturally, this can be more expensive, and protections can vary hugely so pay close attention to the details.

For something more robust such as a washing machine, you might decide breakdown cover is enough if accidental damage is less of a concern.

Our €1,399 4K TV, though, can easily be knocked from its stand, or the screen could get a whack from a sweeping brush or two kids playing catch. This is where an insurance policy might be an option.

Retailer Currys offers “tech insurance” for TVs in different price categories, ranging from €200 to more than €3,000.

For our €1,399 TV the cost would be €180 for a three-year package, and €280 for five years. Monthly payment plans are also on offer if you prefer to spread the cost.

For that, Currys promises to fix the TV within 14 working days and if they don’t meet that deadline, or they’re unable to repair the item, they’ll offer a replacement.

Their website says there is no limit to repairs and if the TV suffers repeated problems, you can seek a new one.

Similar plans are in place for laptops, tablets, cameras, home-cinema set-ups and satellite equipment.

Harvey Norman’s Product Care offers similar cover in two-, three- and four-year plans. It includes things such as “food spoilage cover”, which pays for up to €500 worth of food if a fridge or freezer fails.

Similarly, it offers cover of up to €150 for laundry expenses if your washer or dryer is out of service for more than 10 days after you notify it of the fault.

Are these plans worth it? That’s probably a question only you can answer.

As with any type of insurance, some people are risk-averse and will draw comfort from knowing an unexpected fault or accident will be dealt with. Others might decide they are better off keeping the money in their pocket and taking on the risk themselves.

The price of the appliance matters, but so, too, does your ability to absorb the loss if forced to buy a new item.

Replacing a TV that cost less than €500 might be irritating but manageable, particularly with second-hand options available. Having to find €1,399 – or north of €2,000 for a super high-spec telly – is a completely different story.

You might also want to consider your own track record.

Are you very careful, or are you living in a busy household with children and pets where accidents are more likely to happen?

And before buying any extra protection, make sure to check what it covers.

Currys’ policy, for example, covers sudden accidental damage and mechanical or electrical breakdown. It does not, understandably, extend to cosmetic damage, misuse, neglect or damage during severe weather.

Ultimately, the decision whether to buy will be a combination of your risk appetite, how much the product costs and whether your household budget could absorb the sudden shock of a full replacement.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Breaking down the bill: where does the money you pay for electricity actually go?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/breaking-down-the-bill-where-does-the-money-you-pay-for-electricity-actually-go/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/breaking-down-the-bill-where-does-the-money-you-pay-for-electricity-actually-go/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Irish people pay more for their power than most other Europeans. But no matter how you weigh it, the actual electricity accounts for a far smaller share of your electricity bill than you think.

All in, electricity here costs families around 40 cent a kilowatt hour, the unit in which it sells to domestic customers. That is roughly the energy needed for a typical load in your washing machine. The EU average is 29 cent. Germany is the nearest to us at more than 38 cent.

But that 40 cent ends up going in multiple directions. Energy think-tank Trifecta Ireland estimates that costs other than the actual electricity consume 55 per cent of what Irish homes and industries pay every year.

Those costs range from the money required to get that electricity from power plants to customers to incentives for businesses to build those generators in the first place.

Consultancy Aurora Energy Research calculates that of the €1,583 that an average urban household paid in the 12 months to October 2025, €597, or 32 per cent, covered the price of the electricity, with two-thirds of the total going on associated costs.

Aurora bases its assessment on a home consuming 4,200 kilowatt hours a year, which is what the industry says a typical household uses over 12 months. Those figures pre-date price increases of between 8 and 11 per cent, depending on the supplier, which began to bite this summer. They will have pushed that €1,583 average past €1,700.

Surges in the price of natural gas, which is used to generate half of our electricity, was responsible for those hikes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine has pushed gas prices higher as supply tightens.

But the other costs are creeping up also. Last year, regulators approved plans by national grid operator, Eirgrid, and ESB Networks to spend up to €18.9 billion between now and 2030 on improving the systems that get electricity from power plants to customers. That increase could add up to €1.75 a month to household bills.

More recently, industry watchdog, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilties (CRU), confirmed that emergency generators installed as a backstop against short-term electricity shortages would remain in place up to February 2029. Customers will pay €229 million for this. That scheme will have cost those bill payers €1.44 billion by 2029.

Liberalised

Over the last quarter of a century, the Republic has liberalised its electricity market, merged it with Northern Ireland’s, introduced increasing amounts of wind and solar as it shoulders a large part of meeting the State’s climate targets and shut ageing power plants, all while expecting it to meet increasing demand from economic and population growth.

The policies and strategies meant to deal with all of that have left the State with an increasingly complex system, says Conall Bolger, chief executive of Trifecta Ireland.

“The system we have now wasn’t planned, it sort of evolved rather than being planned, and it’s become unwieldy,” he explains. “We tried to make it do something that it wasn’t built to do.”

Part of the problem is the national grid itself. Stephanie Unsworth, Aurora analyst and author of the consultancy’s recent report on affordability, points out it was built “back in the sixties and seventies”. “Everything then ran on oil and gas,” she says.

At that time, it was a question of connecting power plants, that ran constantly, to where there was demand. It was not designed to link remotely located wind farms than run intermittently to distant cities and towns.

Alongside this, University College Cork academic Paul Deane told the launch of Trifecta’s report this month, electricity is distributed to customers through a large network of copper wire strung on timber poles. This is a legacy issue, according to Deane, who noted that there is enough copper wire in the Irish system to run four times around the globe.

The upshot is that national grid operator Eirgrid is often forced to tell power plants not to supply electricity, even when it is available, as bottlenecks in the system mean it cannot reach customers.

Wind farms, including those in Northern Ireland, are worst hit. This is a double whammy for consumers as alternative suppliers must switch on or increase output even though their power may be more expensive than that of the company unable to operate. Customers pay for this through something called “imperfection charges”, which the CRU says came to €790 million over the last 12 months.

Eirgrid says it is using new technologies to increase its use of renewables and to store power. Following initial trials, it has begun using “dynamic line rating” which allows more effective use of the grid. The State company points out that a planned €18.9 billion investment, approved last year, will tackle many of the problems.

Customers also face a bill of €550 million to support gas-fired power stations when they are on standby to back up renewables, but not supplying electricity, and so not earning money. These “capacity payments” are an incentive to encourage developers to build these plants in the first place.

Unsworth notes that many of the extra charges are the price customers pay as they foot the bill for integrating renewables into a system designed for fossil fuel. He does agree that the plans by Eirgrid and ESB Networks to invest in the system over the next four years should help.

Trifecta, funded by the family of industry veteran, Eddie O’Connor, focuses on providing affordable, secure and clean electricity. Its report, What Can Move the Needle on Bills Before 2030?, assesses ways of cutting costs to the consumer in the shorter term.

Its CEO, Bolger believes that we need to step back and look at all elements of the system in their entirety. He argues that the needs of consumers got lost while government and State agencies increasingly added complexity to the system. But cutting bills in the absence of a major overhaul remains challenging.

Deane told the Trifecta launch that, in some cases, cutting €10 from bills could require spending of €100 million on the system.

Trifecta proposes 17 smaller measures that it says should add up to greater savings. They focus on more efficient use of the grid that takes more account of customers’ needs. More electrification of heat and transport should help, the organisation says. This is because many of the “non-electric” costs are fixed, so spreading the burden across more customers cuts individual burdens.

Unsworth agrees that more electrification is part of the solution, but with a different emphasis. Instead of focusing on “crazy” renewables targets, she advocates building power plants to meet demand while incentivising electrification, which would still allow the Republic to meet its climate targets. Aurora calculates that taking this alternative approach would cost consumers 20 per cent less by 2035 than if we continue with our current mix of strategies.

How your electricity bill adds up

Generation: This is the cost of producing the electricity we use. It is generated by burning natural gas, or by wind and solar farms, along with contributions from other sources, including imports and hydroelectric power.

This amounts to a lower portion of bills than most people assume. A recent report by Trifecta Ireland calculates it at 45 per cent across the board. A breakdown of charges for a typical home by consultancy Aurora Energy Research shows it came to €597 out of a total annual average bill of €1,583, or around 38 per cent, in the 12 months to October 2025.

Network: This is the cost of getting electricity from power plants to homes and businesses. Basically, it goes through two stages. The national grid takes the electricity direct from power stations, and the distribution network takes it from the national grid and transmits it to customers’ premises. This cost is itemised as a standing charge on electricity bills, generally coming to around one-third of the total.

Aurora calculates that this cost its typical home €443 last year. Energy industry overseer, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is currently reviewing how these costs are allocated across electricity customers.

Public Service Obligation (PSO): This pays for schemes that guarantee prices for power produced by renewable power plants. Two account for most of this charge. The first is the Renewable Energy Feed-in Tariff, which guarantees older onshore wind farms €72 or €75 per mega-watt hour for their electricity. If the market price falls below that figure, customers make up the difference through the PSO levy. If the market price is higher, the renewable power companies keep any surplus.

The second is the Renewable Energy Support Scheme, which pays wind and solar farms prices agreed at various auctions. Customers make up the difference if the market price falls short but get a rebate if the market price tops the guaranteed amounts.

The CRU recently set the PSO at €6.12 for each household in total for the coming 12 months, a sharp reduction on what they paid between October 2025 and this month. The charge is itemised on domestic bills.

Imperfection charge: This is one of two big items not set out on your bill. It is the cost of bottlenecks on the national grid that prevent it from transmitting electricity generated in one place to where the customers are located. In this situation, national grid operator, Eirgrid, instructs the power plant to reduce output. The market compensates the supplier for this. At the same time, the grid may have to instruct other companies whose electricity can reach those customers to step in. Those companies are also paid for their power.

Industry organisations have been highlighting this problem for a while. Most often, it hits wind farms in the west or other locations far from the greater Dublin area, where demand for electricity is greatest.

One significant bottleneck is the continued absence of a planned high-capacity power line between counties Meath and Tyrone. This prevents wind farms and other suppliers in the North from getting their electricity to the South. All electricity customers share this cost. Overall, CRU approved €790.24 million for imperfection charges over the last 12 months. Aurora calculates that it added €67 to individual bills last year.

Capacity payments: These are incentives to suppliers to build gas-fired power plants. Wind and solar power are not available all the time so our system needs gas plants that can be switched on or off quickly to back them up.

As these power stations do not run all the time, their owners cannot recover their costs simply by selling electricity, so they receive capacity payments for ensuring that they are available to supply power, even when they are not doing so. All electricity customers also share this cost. The CRU allowed €550 million in capacity payments over the last 12 months. Aurora says it cost the typical family €75 last year.

VAT and other costs: Domestic customers pay 9 per cent VAT on electricity, which would have come to €142.47 on the €1,583 that Aurora calculates a typical suburban Irish home for electricity last year. The consultancy estimates that the tax, along with supplier and market costs, accounted for €362 of that total, more than 20 per cent.

Second, the AI investment boom faces three big constraints: financial, physical and political.

Financial constraints led the recent AI jitters, as investors increasingly questioned whether the returns on huge AI investments would justify the spending and whether enough capital would be available to finance it all. ]]><![CDATA[The career costs of non-competes: ‘Your star striker is sitting on the bench’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/30/non-compete-clauses-employment-law-work-rival-employers-united-kingdom-andy-burnham/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/30/non-compete-clauses-employment-law-work-rival-employers-united-kingdom-andy-burnham/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Damien Couture remembers going through “seven, eight months of hell” with his family after he was sued by his former hedge fund employer for allegedly breaching a non-compete agreement when he left to join a rival.

The issue of non-competes has shot to prominence in the United Kingdom after prime minister Andy Burnham this month pledged to introduce legislation to ensure such clauses could “no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising start-ups and scaling firms”.

More than five million British workers have non-competes in their employment contracts that prevent them moving to a competitor for a period after leaving their job.

“Non-competes can give ... comfort that people are not just going to walk out the door and join or set up a rival using the intellectual property they have gained at the company,” says Amy Bird, a partner in the employment team of law firm Clifford Chance.

Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?

Citadel, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, successfully lobbied last year for legislation in its home state of Florida to allow non-compete agreements lasting up to four years.

While highly paid fund managers often appreciate the chance to take time off and travel or spend time with their family, such lengthy non-compete periods can make top performers less attractive to other employers, limiting the opportunities to seek out better and higher-paid roles.

Workers are usually unpaid during the period in the UK at least, and their skills may fall behind those of their peers, particularly in fast-growing sectors.

Burnham said the clauses “stunt innovation and trap workers” because these “prevent the best really being energised and bringing that dynamism to the economy”.

The UK’s tech sector has criticised non-competes for making it harder for them to hire. More than 20 start-up founders recently wrote to Burnham to ask him to “ban lengthy post-termination restrictions”.

Alan Chang, founder of the $5 billion (€4.5 billion) energy start-up Fuse and co-signatory of the letter, says his company’s progress has been slowed because of the delay in hiring caused by non-competes and other employment restrictions.

Chang says his chief technology officer, Greg Wilk, was originally subject to an 18-month non-compete clause. This was reduced to six months of gardening leave – which differs from a non-compete period as the person remains a paid employee – before he joined Fuse because he was changing industry.

But Chang says the wait was still too long. “Let’s say [Wilk joined in] one month rather than six ... I think our share price [would] be worth a lot more ... And rather than us being in two markets, we [would be] in four markets.”

Jacomo Corbo, founder of $2.4 billion start-up PhysicsX, says he is currently negotiating a 15-month non-compete agreement to hire an employee, an experience that has made him consider recruiting more in the US where restrictions are less prevalent.

“In Europe ... on the whole, you find that these long notice periods and gardening leave are very prevalent,” he says. “The lack of liquidity means you end up refocusing a lot of that hiring on US hires.”

Edward Hughes, who had a three-month gardening leave after leaving Google DeepMind to co-found London-based artificial intelligence (AI) start-up Inherent, which co-ordinated the letter to Burnham, says restrictions risk leaving fast-growing companies a “generation” behind their Californian competitors.

Burnham did not give full details of the reform he is planning, but said the aim was to free up hiring for innovative companies, including in the AI sector.

The UK is an outlier in having relatively few constraints on employers’ use of non-competes, although they must show a clause is reasonable to enforce it in court. Elsewhere, efforts to curb the use of non-competes have had mixed results: a long-standing ban in California has not stopped some employers writing the clauses into contracts, even though these cannot be upheld by law.

Spain can fine employers that use them wrongly; France requires companies to continue paying staff part of their salary during non-compete periods. Australia plans to limit their use to high earners.

Shivchand Jhinku, an employment partner at law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer in Sydney, says an unintended consequence of restricting non-competes in Australia may be to benefit bigger companies that have more ways to compete for staff, such as the ability to pay more and offer better perks.

“Smaller businesses and start-ups, which often rely on non-competes as the only practical mechanism to protect their investment in key employees, may be less able to compete for talent,” he says.

Lawyers predict the curbing of non-competes in the UK may lead employers to use other tools to protect their intellectual property and delay the departure of employees. In their letter to Burnham, the tech founders also argued for the restriction of “extended notice periods and gardening leave”.

Another downside to non-competes is that disputes over the terms often result in costly and stressful legal contests.

Citadel, for example, this year launched a lawsuit against its former portfolio manager Daniel Shatz, who left to join UK rival Marshall Wace.

London-based quant trader Couture was sued by Jump Trading in 2023 after telling the Chicago-headquartered firm he was joining rival Verition Fund Management. He had already served a 12-month notice period after resigning, but his contract also included an extra non-compete period of up to a year, which Jump insisted he respected.

The 41-year-old reached a confidential settlement with Jump that allowed him to continue working at Verition, but only after he had spent almost £1 million (€1.2 million) on lawyers to defend himself in court. “It was a huge stress,” he says. “Anxiety for the whole family went through the roof.”

Couture still believes non-compete clauses can play a valuable role, but thinks they should have a time limit placed on them by law. “The fact that UK law does not express up to what point they are reasonable makes it a matter to be determined by a judge, where individuals have to face deep-pocketed companies,” he says.

Faced with increasing risks to the growth and inflation outlook, the ECB needs to ensure the smooth transmission of its monetary stance and a smooth transition in leadership.

The ECB has been in similar situations before, but this time looks different regarding the inflation outlook, geopolitical context and personnel dynamics.

Energy prices remain elevated and early signs of the second-round effects of that on consumer prices are emerging. While underlying inflationary and wage pressures have remained contained for now, they have not eased either.

Candidates to replace ECB president Christine Lagarde

The latest ECB bank lending survey suggests banks are already tightening lending standards, while demand for new loans is weakening.

Higher borrowing costs and tighter credit conditions should reduce the need for further increases in policy rates, all else equal, but the ECB is facing a bigger communication challenge.

Alternatively, any hint that the bank may activate the bond-buying tool known as the transmission protection instrument (TPI) would risk making French problems worse. Tweaking the TPI conditionality to make France eligible may be politically toxic in other countries.

He also served one six-year term as ‌the Bank of Spain governor from 2018 to 2024, a tumultuous ​period that started with ultra-low inflation, followed by the pandemic and a historic interest rate hike cycle to tame runaway inflation.

]]>The Washington Post<![CDATA[Farewell to ‘aeroplane mode’: Flying loses its status as the last internet black hole]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/29/easyjet-internet-in-flight-wifi-starlink-elon-musk-aer-lingus-ryanair-short-haul/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/29/easyjet-internet-in-flight-wifi-starlink-elon-musk-aer-lingus-ryanair-short-haul/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:00:01 +0000Back in 1997, an episode of Seinfeld introduced the world to a unique approach to long-haul travel. David Puddy, played by Patrick Warburton, the boyfriend of Elaine Benes (Julia Louis Dreyfus), decided he would just stare at the back of the seat in front of him for the whole flight.

No television, no movies, no headphones, no books, not even a nap. He was going to sit upright, eyes-open, and stare straight ahead for what was meant to be a very long trip.

Although this was wild even to contemplate almost three decades ago, it isn’t viewed in quite so simple a light today.

Is airplane mode really just a setting on your phone? That’s the philosophical question that has moved to the foreground in recent days.

On Monday, EasyJet announced it would install Elon Musk’s Starlink internet across its fleet during the first half of next year, with roll-out completed in 2028.

Aer Lingus already offers Starlink on its transatlantic flights with plans eventually to extend it to European flights.

The jump from wifi of any standard on a plane being impressive to high speed being the norm has come about rather quickly.

Aer Lingus has begun its free in-flight wifi. Bang goes a rare oasis of tranquillity

Airline wifi has, for most of the 20 years it has been available, been somewhat of a joke. Typically it has been considered slow, expensive and definitely not reliable. Yet that’s far too broad an assumption.

Even back in 2019, I recall an Air France trip back from China where I was overjoyed that the quality was good enough to watch Dublin beat Mayo in the All Ireland semi-final. Still, that was definitely the exception, not the norm.

With Starlink’s satellites orbiting around 550 kilometres above ground, they are shortening the journey that was previously needed for signals to reach planes.

With the Aer Lingus transatlantic fleet as an example, the speeds promised exceed 500Mbps. When it comes to connectivity quality, that’s absolutely stellar stuff.

With EasyJet, well it’s essentially the same service only focused squarely on short-haul. That is rather new as plane wifi has thus far almost exclusively been targeted at long-haul by carriers in Europe.

It is a huge step for wifi to go from being an available extra service towards it being expected on all journeys in the not-too-distant future. It’s heavenly to some of you and no doubt a nightmare to others.

That’s because the last acceptable excuse for being unreachable is disappearing. An aeroplane is one of the few places where you have outright immunity from checking emails or messages. That’s from everyone in your life, although, for most of us, the first thing to come to mind is work.

“I’m 35,000 feet above ground embracing the engineering miracle of mechanised flight” won’t necessarily be considered a good enough excuse any more.

Yet the benefits are substantial. That game I watched back in 2019 was exactly what I needed. I’d just spent a couple of hours in Hong Kong airport interviewing protesters and it was emotionally moving and draining. Being able to decompress by watching Con O’Callaghan and Paul Mannion run riot was the best possible thing for me at the time.

There’s also the matter of parents travelling with children. As a child-free person, I was surprised by how popular YouTube premium is with parents. Several have told me it’s the last subscription they would consider giving up. For them it is a reliable way to make sure their kids have access to their favourite videos while travelling. Getting that access on planes only adds to that support for parents.

Connectivity doesn’t have to be about productivity. An employer who expects you to stay connected with work when you’re on a plane probably has a lot more wrong with them than just that.

Smart bosses know that rest matters. Even remotely intelligent ones know that flights are tiring in and of themselves, so it’s not like you’re getting a net productivity benefit by irking staff while they’re strapped to a seat high above the ground.

Retaining the ability to disconnect should not come down to whether there actually is a connection.

Not everyone agrees with the move to connect and that includes airlines. For the foreseeable future, Ryanair is not going to embrace Starlink.

Michael O’Leary has said plainly that he felt the cost/benefit analysis just did not compute for his airline.

Still, where it is an option, it’s important that people remember that an option means they have a choice.

Warburton has jokingly apologised for his character kicking off the unfortunately named “rawdogging” trend. This, however, is not a choice of extremes. Those who feel the need to stare at the back of a chair still can, while, in the near future, those who want optimal connectivity will have it.

Everything in between is also on the table and a matter of free will. You can just watch a movie on the screen, follow the map or listen to something downloaded on your phone. You’ll simply have more choices as to what you can do.

If your concern is not being able to disconnect, then you really shouldn’t blame the airline. Instead, ask who or what in your work or personal life makes you feel the need to be always on. Then address that deeper issue, which is beyond Aer Lingus’ or EasyJet’s pay grade.

We have been letting our holiday home for more than two years to a Ukrainian family under the Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) scheme. The Government is ending the scheme in March 2027.

The reader has availed of the tax-free Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP), now paid at €400 a month, for accommodating a Ukrainian family in her holiday home.

There were 16,300 people hosting 38,300 Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection as of October 11th, according to the Department of Justice.

Occupants under the ARP scheme are regarded as licensees rather than tenants, says Shane O’Dea, a senior solicitor at Amorys Solicitors.

“Hosting under the ARP is not a formal landlord/tenant relationship, so they have no landlord/tenant rights at the moment,” says O’Dea.

If no additional payments were made to the landlord by their ARP occupant, then no tenancy existed under the Residential Tenancies Act, says the Residential Tenancies Board.

The reader says she would be happy for her Ukrainian friends to continue living in her holiday home after the ARP scheme ends in March. She would plan to charge a modest rent but this would constitute a tenancy, which, according to RTB rules, would begin from the date that rent became payable by a tenant.

New private rental sector tenancy rules mean the reader would be restricted in how she could end that tenancy.

Tenancies created since March 1st this year are subject to rolling six-year tenancies of minimum duration.

A landlord can end a new tenancy in the first six months for any reason, says the RTB. But after six months, they must have specific reasons to do so.

“If a tenant has been renting a property for six months and they haven’t received a valid notice of termination, a landlord can only end the tenancy during the six years on very limited grounds,” says O’Dea.

The specific conditions are linked to how many tenancies the landlord has.

All landlords can end a tenancy during the six years if the tenant doesn’t meet their obligations, such as paying rent.

Small landlords – those with between with one and three tenancies – can avail of additional grounds for ending a tenancy. These are if they need to sell due to financial hardship or if they or a close family member, such as a spouse, civil partner, parent, parent-in-law or child, wants to use the property as a primary residence.

Using the property as a holiday home is not one of the reasons under which a tenancy can be ended.

If the reader decides to end the new tenancy during the first six months, dates are really important. She must give the tenant between 90 and 120 days’ notice and a copy of the notice of termination must also be sent to the RTB within seven days of the date it is served.

The holiday homeowner and the Ukrainian family clearly have a good relationship, so they could agree to a “break” option after a certain amount of time, says O’Dea.

“For example, the property owner could include the option to terminate the lease after a year or two if the tenant signs up to that,” he says, “but if the landlord exercises the break option and the tenant refuses to leave, the break option is totally unenforceable.”

“It’s only in good faith that you do that between two parties but if the tenant refuses to comply, they have all the rights.”

Agreeing a fixed-term tenancy for a specified period does not overrule a tenant’s rights, the RTB advises.

No matter the stated duration of the fixed-term lease, once the tenant has lived in the property for six months with no valid notice of termination, they have security of tenure and can remain in the property, it says.

“Once they are in the property for six months after March 31st, 2027, then they can remain there for six years,” says O’Dea.

If she sets a modest rent, this can only be increased once a year by 2 per cent, or the rate of inflation, whichever is lowest.

She can only reset the rent to market value at the beginning of a new tenancy, but only if the last tenancy ended because the tenant left by choice, the tenant breached their obligations or at the end of a six-year tenancy of minimum duration cycle for an ongoing tenancy.

AIB’s report contained a mini-analysis of the current turmoil in bond markets.

“Overall, the OECD estimates that the G7 countries spent around 2.1 per cent of GDP on interest payments in 2025,” it said.

“This was forecast to rise to 2.3 per cent on average this year, but it will now be higher following the surge in government bond yields,” it said.

“This will have real economic consequences, particularly as populations continue to age at a time when many countries are spending more on defence, energy and other areas,” the report said.

International investors give Ireland the thumbs up, ignoring corporate tax warnings

After playing a stellar, if unwanted, role in the 2008 financial crisis, Ireland now finds itself at one remove from the financial challenge of the day courtesy of record corporate tax receipts.

AIB noted that Government is set to run a large budget surplus once again in 2026.

As a result of this, the spread between Irish and German 10-year yields has actually narrowed slightly to just 13 basis points – or 0.13 of a percentage point.

“This implies Ireland is very firmly within the ”core" group of European countries alongside Germany, Netherlands and Luxembourg,” AIB said.

Without Ireland’s corporate tax bonanza, the economic atmosphere in the State would be entirely different.

The Department of Finance forecasts that the State’s surplus this year would turn to a deficit of €12.1 billion (3.4 per cent of national income) if windfall corporation tax receipts were excluded, rising to a deficit of €20.3 billion (4.6 per cent of national income) by 2030.

“The lesson is [that] Ireland cannot take its success for granted, and the recent memory of bond markets souring on our debt highlights how quickly sovereigns can lose credibility,” AIB said.

Increasingly, organisations are offering employee benefits such as financial assistance with fertility treatment and egg freezing but, culturally and behaviourally, they are lagging behind in supporting workers who choose these options, according to researchers at DCU’s Institute for Business and Society.

Pregnancy and parenthood can be a time of great joy and anticipation but for those having trouble conceiving – or those who have miscarried – it can be filled with anxiety, fear and even shame.

Organisational behaviour specialist Céire Gilsenan experienced all these emotions and more when she was going through her first fertility journey while working full-time. She kept the circle of trust small so, besides her partner, only her sister knew she was undergoing IVF.

At work, she slipped out surreptitiously for doctor’s appointments and for phone calls about her results.

“I remember distinctly sitting in the clinic, just feeling so uncomfortable and pretending to read the paper because I was terrified of seeing somebody that I knew. I was physically sweating because I knew I was going to be late back to work, and you’re trying to think of an excuse of where you were.”

Gilsenan felt extremely vulnerable as her high-pressure workplace clashed with the demands of intensive medical protocols. Her experience is not that unusual, according to researchers.

“Work and motherhood are never more on a collision than they are during fertility treatment,” says Prof Yseult Freeney of DCU, who studies women in the workplace. “Fertility treatment is like a second job. It’s a second shift, but it’s one that they can’t control because they don’t know when it’s going to happen. They also really can’t control when they’re going to get bad news.”

Fertility treatment and the workplace: ‘It’s a hugely personal thing to have to say’

For partners, Freeney says, they’re often “meant to be the strong person in this, but the challenges for them are equally hard, just different. They’re not as physical but they’re absolutely as emotional.”

A VHI survey, Fertility in Focus: The Workplace Realities, found that 14 per cent of women surveyed in 2024 had experienced fertility issues. Of those, two-thirds said it had interfered with work, while only 20 per cent felt prepared and 64 per cent feared future health problems if their stress continued.

Of the respondents, only 27 per cent had spoken to their employer and 74 per cent had sought advice from their GP.

Gilsenan’s decision not to reveal her situation to her colleagues or wider family was deliberate. “I felt that if it didn’t go well, I wouldn’t be able to deal with my own distress and handle other people’s distress or reaction to my distress.”

Her fertility journey was ultimately successful. Afterwards she decided to research this emerging area further. She was the lead author on Experiencing and Responding to Existential Vulnerability: Navigating the Work–Fertility Treatment Interface, published in the Gender, Work and Organisation Journal. Gilsenan was supervised by Freeney and assisted by fellow researchers Lisa van der Werff and Hilary O’Leary of DCU’s Institute for Business and Society.

Gilsenan interviewed 18 other women who had undergone fertility treatment while working full-time. “People had miscarriages and went back to work the next day. They got phone calls at work to say that the treatment hadn’t worked for the third or fourth time and just went back out of that meeting room and into the office like everything was normal.”

Although fertility treatment was gruelling physically and emotionally, all felt it was important to maintain a professional identity. Their desire to work, and be recognised at work, did not pause just because they were trying to become parents.

Whether or not the woman chose to reveal her fertility treatment to family or colleagues, the research found that feelings of vulnerability were common, and the women navigated the work-fertility interface in three distinct ways: masking, confronting and succumbing.

  • Masking is the exhausting, active pretence of hiding your physical and emotional distress to protect a professional image. This was the most common response and included hiding appointments, overworking, crying in the toilet and then presenting a brave face in public. Freeney says there’s a feeling among the women that “they can’t put all their eggs in one basket. So, ‘If this is not going to work out, I have to have something else to fall back on’. They then overinvest in work by adopting a masking response.”
  • Confronting is when the woman decides to tell a trusted manager or colleague and reclaim some control over her life and time. This helps them set shared boundaries and expectations around appointments and calls. For example, Gilsenan revealed the situation to a concerned colleague, and this provided great relief. “She would cover for me and she even came to the clinic with me a few times. It genuinely did make a world of difference.”
  • Succumbing is when the hopeful parent reaches a point of being overwhelmed and can no longer manage their vulnerability, says Freeney. Their capacity to cope has been exceeded and they might start stepping back from projects and feel a profound loss of hope.

One interviewee recounted her first performance review after treatment ended. She told her manager: “Stop talking to me about performance. I don’t care about it any more. I have no one to put through college.”

The paper finds that telling a manager, member of HR or a colleague doesn’t end the vulnerability or distress, and many keep masking even after telling someone.

Gilsenan said of the medical process: “I’ll inject myself a million times. I’ll go through those awful tests and procedures. It didn’t take a jot out of me.” The hard part, she says, was the “anguish of the whole thing, the uncertainty, how vulnerable you are, how unpredictable it is”.

Workplace wellbeing and productivity go hand in hand, so offering to pay for fertility benefits isn’t enough on its own. Organisations should foster compassionate, informed workplace cultures that support employee wellbeing, engagement and retention while reducing the stigma often associated with fertility challenges.

The DCU researchers hope that by making this hidden dimension of working life visible, organisations will build cultures that reduce the weight of existential vulnerability for aspiring parents.

‘Injecting yourself daily is difficult to navigate at work’: Managing fertility treatment while working

Creating fertility-aware workplaces doesn’t mean having all the answers. “You don’t need a policy to lead with empathy and compassion,” says Gilsenan.

Often, the most meaningful support begins with awareness and flexibility for those undergoing treatment. Women shouldn’t have to make up lies to cover appointments, says Freeney. The work is getting done; they just need some flexibility.

“Employees who feel supported by their employer during significant life experiences are more likely to remain engaged, loyal and connected to their organisation. In contrast, employees who feel they must hide their fertility journey may experience increased stress, absenteeism, disengagement and isolation,” says the Sims IVF clinic.

VHI recommends stress supports and counselling, fertility education talks, including fertility in wellness programmes, and flexible working and leave.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

It is not exactly news that, nowadays, that era seems like a quaint and distant memory.

Perhaps that’s why some of the allegations made about Meta during the recent Brazilian election so captured the electorate’s attention.

The owner of Facebook, Instagram and Whatsapp became a huge election talking point when Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign requested that his rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, be disqualified before the final round of voting over the weekend due to interference by Meta.

In a court petition, Lula’s team complained that the tech giant had favoured his right-wing opponent’s content over his, giving Bolsonaro an advantage. Among other things, they claimed that for a 24-hour period, Lula was unable to boost his Instagram posts, while Bolsonaro could. Several watchdogs and human rights groups also said they found evidence of bias in Meta’s algorithm.

Meta denies the claims and called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”. It said there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.

It’s not clear to which incidents Meta is referring. Yet, as early as August, Amnesty International was warning that election adverts containing disinformation were slipping through the cracks in Meta’s monitoring systems.

While it didn’t make an allegation of bias, the human rights group said at that time that it found Facebook had “approved eight ads that contained disinformation”. Of the eight, “four focused solely on ‘electoral delegitimisation’, two were solely from the ‘security-focused authoritarianism’ category, including disinformation advocating military intervention or non-participation in elections. The other two overlapped between the three categories”.

Brazilians in Ireland turn out in force for presidential vote

The more recent controversy in Brazil was prompted by Meta’s oversight board’s “over-enforcement of Meta’s fraud policies against Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s ad accounts” on a particular date during the campaign. Apparently, this happened “by mistake ... and not for political reasons.”

Malice or incompetence: whatever the reason, the outsize influence that powerful tech companies can have on elections has been a talking point for some years. With the billionaire owners behind them cosying up to the likes of Donald Trump, it cannot be ignored any longer.

]]>Nelson Almeida<![CDATA[Meet the Irish AI app aiming to end the chaos of organising family life ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/10/29/meet-the-irish-ai-app-aiming-to-end-the-chaos-of-organising-family-life/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/10/29/meet-the-irish-ai-app-aiming-to-end-the-chaos-of-organising-family-life/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 03:15:00 +0000James Foskin left school at 17 and went straight into the workforce. He spent a decade in customer-facing roles across different sectors before someone told him about a new company setting up in Ireland.

It turned out to be PayPal, and Foskin was one of its first employees. He subsequently spent just over 20 years with the company, progressing up the ladder to director level.

In 2025, Foskin left PayPal to set up TiAiMe: the name stands for Ti (time), Ai (the AI engine), Me (the priority person).

It’s a life co-ordination platform designed for today’s time-pressed adults who wear multiple hats as parents, carers, professionals, diary coordinators, housekeepers and kids’ taxi.

He got the idea from watching work colleagues struggle to manage their busy lives and from seeing his wife try to keep a dozen different balls in the air when their son was ill and needed a lot of care.

“As a leader, a colleague, a coach and a parent, I had an unfiltered view of one of the most persistent problems of modern life: we are more time-poor now than ever before despite advances in technology,” Foskin says.

“This is not because people are failing. It is because the systems built to support them are failing them. Many families are using up to seven-plus systems to manage their lives, but none of them talk to each other, further adding to the mental overload. TiAiMe co-ordinates a user’s life and support network through one connected system with child protection embedded by design and human authority always overriding AI.

“Every existing tool was built for a different job,” Foskin adds.

“Calendars manage one person’s time. Family apps help one household remember plans but cannot rearrange them when life changes. AI assistants serve one person with no family layer. New AI entrants solve one slice of the problem. Every single one stops at the same wall – one person, one household, one bit of life. None co-ordinate with the people around you. None talk to each other.”

Foskin stresses that TiAiMe is not just another time management or productivity tool. Instead, he describes it as an operating system for contemporary living that works as an “intelligent AI life partner”, or a digital self that learns about a user’s routines, commitments and family structure (through an onboarding survey initially) to help lower the stress factor and avoid panics and clashes when events collide.

Limerick start-up uses AI to take the pain out of compliance

For example, a parent delayed picking up a child from school can ask TiAiMe (much like talking to Siri) to find someone in their network who is free to collect the child instead. Whoever is free verbally confirms their availability to TiAiMe, which sends them the details and confirms the pickup with the parent. “What you get is one school pickup, co-ordinated end-to-end without the time-consuming back and forth of a group chat,” Foskin says.

“I have worked with many talented, capable people who were quietly overwhelmed by the invisible weight of keeping everything together,” he says. “Work, family, health, relationships. All of it managed across a tangle of disconnected tools that were never designed to work together. Watching talented female colleagues in particular wrestle with the impossible balance between career and home never left me, but I kept hitting the same wall. The tool that could truly solve this did not exist. So, I set about building it.”

Before starting to design TiAiMe, Foskin spent months talking to 175 time-pressed families about their lived experience of constantly being in a rush. “What came back was a demand,” Foskin says. “Please don’t build another app. We are already using multiple systems. Please just build one system that works across our whole life.

“Our research showed that 84 per cent of adults find co-ordinating family and support network schedules genuinely difficult,” Foskin says.

“In addition, they spend most of their time reacting to urgent demands rather than living the life they actually want. Dreams or life goals are on hold for a time that rarely arrives. It’s time for a disruptive approach to help us stop reacting to life and start building and living our lives with intent by seeing time as the enabler.”

Already 50 families have taken part in a pre-launch pilot, in advance of November’s full launch.

Foskin says the app doesn’t so much have customer types as pressure types – as in those carrying multiple responsibilities. For example, a working parent who is also looking after ageing relatives.

To date, Foskin has spent around €60,000 developing the platform, and a pre-seed start fund application is currently pending with Enterprise Ireland.

He is now looking to recruit two equity co-founders to fulfil the roles of chief technical officer and chief commercial officer and would particularly like to bring a woman co-founder on board who could bring her life experience to further developing the platform. Foskin’s ambition for the business is global, with the first phase targeting Ireland, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and the United States.

Humans must always be responsible for AI

Asked if leaving PayPal to take a leap into the unknown was difficult, Foskin says, “The shift from a structured corporate environment with its teams, its resources, its monthly salary and its daily rhythm to sitting alone building a company from scratch is something nobody fully prepares you for. The isolation and loneliness of being a solo founder hit harder than I expected.

“You go from leading teams and being surrounded by people every day to making every decision alone. But I had a fantastic technical development partner in RaftLabs, and the real turning point for me was being accepted on to the tech accelerator, run by David Slowey.

“David doesn’t talk about an MVP (minimum viable product). He talks about a minimum viable business and having someone who challenged me hard when I needed it changed everything,” Foskin says.

“Leaning into the experience gained from the 50+ programmes designed and deployed from scratch during my PayPal years had shown me one thing clearly: I knew how to take something from blank page to full roll-out. Two decades building someone else’s vision had been invaluable, but it was time to build my own.”
