AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:09:28 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 How Condor’s post-Lufthansa ‘Plan B’ is paying off https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/condor-expansion-fleet-lufthansa-routes/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54811 Condor’s post-Lufthansa strategy is gaining momentum, with new feeder routes, rising load factors and expanding airline partnerships.

The post How Condor’s post-Lufthansa ‘Plan B’ is paying off appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Condor turned a major Lufthansa setback into growth, building its own feeder network to keep long-haul flights full.
  • CEO Peter Gerber says the airline’s new city routes are outperforming expectations and attracting lucrative corporate travellers.
  • With American Airlines, Alaska and JetBlue partnerships growing, Condor is positioning itself as a stronger independent competitor.

Condor has established a new European feeder network following the loss of its long-standing arrangement with Lufthansa, with load factors above 70% on its city routes as the German carrier seeks to strengthen its long-haul operation at Frankfurt.

Chief executive Peter Gerber said at Routes World 2026 – being hosted in the German financial capital – that the carrier had been forced to move quickly after a court decision meant it could no longer rely on Lufthansa’s network to supply connecting passengers for its long-haul flights.

Condor’s secret ‘Plan B’ after Lufthansa tie-up collapsed

The development had come as a surprise, he said, but Condor had already been preparing an alternative strategy in case its agreement with Lufthansa could not be extended.

“We worked secretly on a plan B, just in case it turned out like it did,” he said. “It was absolutely clear that we need to do something about it because if you have such a huge long haul fleet as Condor, and you have the geographic situation in Germany, obviously you can’t operate long haul fleets without a feed.”

Gerber said the airline initially concentrated on establishing connections within Germany and German-speaking markets before expanding into other destinations as airport slots became available.

The new network has also required Condor to re-establish itself as a different entity for passengers. While the airline has historically positioned itself as a leisure carrier, it is now seeking to attract passengers travelling between European cities, including corporate customers who can provide additional traffic for its long-haul services.

A return to the Lufthansa arrangement remains uncertain, Gerber said, with the outcome dependent on the courts and competition authorities. Condor is planning to operate without it, adding: “We have to plan on our own.”

Condor city network attracts corporate travellers

Gerber said the initial performance of the network had exceeded his expectations, with load factors above 70%.

Gerber said customer experience had been central to that effort, alongside advertising and the airline’s online presence. “People start to tell this to their friends, and we increasingly get more corporate contracts.”

Rather than attempting to replicate the breadth of Lufthansa’s domestic and European network, Gerber said Condor was concentrating on destinations that generate the most valuable connecting traffic.

“We will never be able to build up the broadness of the Lufthansa network,” he said. Instead, the airline is focusing on “the most important O&D destinations for our customers”, while adding the routes and slots needed to serve those markets.

He said the airline intends to continue developing Frankfurt as its principal hub, arguing that the economics and geography of Germany make it difficult to establish another comparable operation elsewhere in the country.

A second German hub would be harder to make work, Gerber said, because it depends on having enough customers nearby and on airport operating conditions. “The only second opportunity to run such a kind of a hub in Germany would be Dusseldorf,” he said, adding that the airport’s operating limits make it difficult.

American Airlines partnership opens new markets

Commercial partnerships are becoming increasingly important as Condor expands beyond its traditional leisure model.

Gerber highlighted the airline’s relationship with American Airlines, which he expects to support the development of services to Chicago by providing connecting traffic on both sides of the Atlantic.

He said this partnership worked for both parties. “We offer American a good opportunity to really be more present in Europe. So that’s a clear win-win situation.”

Condor also works with partners including Alaska Airlines and JetBlue, alongside carriers in South Africa and Asia. Gerber said these arrangements were helping passengers make more seamless connecting journeys while providing Condor with access to markets it could not serve as effectively on its own.

The airline is also considering whether joining an alliance could be a logical next step as its transformation progresses.

“I think it’s clear that we will look into that after we now more or less in principle completed our transformation, and so this could be a next logical step to expand the reach of Condor,” he told Routes delegates.

For the time being, the carrier intends to develop its existing partnerships without an alliance commitment.

Growth ambitions face pressure from costs

Despite the progress in rebuilding its network, Condor faces pressure from high operating costs in Germany and rising fuel prices.

Gerber said the airline remained ambitious about expanding both its long-haul and leisure operations, with winter demand for long-haul destinations performing particularly well. However, he warned that higher fares were becoming a constraint on some European routes.

The airline is also pursuing a €100m savings target, with Gerber saying it had reached agreements with employees and unions to support its expansion plans. 

Around two-thirds of the savings would come from contract management and efficiency measures.

Gerber said Condor had performed well operationally during the summer, particularly on routes to destinations including Bangkok and Phuket, but that higher fuel prices had impacted their financial results, especially compared with forecasts made at the beginning of the year.

]]> Italy’s new M-346 aerobatic jet takes flight for first time with striking new livery https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/italian-air-force-frecce-tricolori-m-346-aerobatic-team-new-livery/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:04:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55085 The first M-346 built for the Italian Air Force’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team has made its maiden flight with a brand new livery

The post Italy’s new M-346 aerobatic jet takes flight for first time with striking new livery appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 2 min read
  • The first M-346 built for Italy's Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team has completed its maiden flight, sporting a striking new tricolour livery.
  • The advanced twin-engine jet will replace the team's ageing MB-339 aircraft, marking a major fleet modernisation programme.
  • Operational deliveries are expected from 2027, with the Frecce Tricolori's first full display season on the M-346 planned for 2028.

Sporting the colours of the Italian flag, the first M-346 built for the Italian Air Force’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team made its maiden flight on 29 October.

Marking a milestone in the Frecce Tricolori’s transition to a new generation of aircraft, airframe manufacturer Leonardo rolled out the M-346 at its plant in Venengono near Varese on 16 October. Photos of the jet first emerged the following day and show it already carrying the new livery.

However, it still lacks its number and the Frecce Tricolori markings on its tail, according to The Aviationist.

The livery combines the three colours of the national flag with dark blue. It was designed by the Italian firm Pininfarina and first shown to the public in 2024. The Italian Air Force describes it as developing the theme of the “renaissance of the tricolor.”  

A new era for the Frecce Tricolori team

The M-346 will replace the MB-339s flown by the national aerobatic team since 1982. The decision to renew the fleet was announced in September 2024 at Istrana air base as the team returned from a display tour of the US. The twin-engine M-346 was chosen over an earlier plan to opt for the single-engine M-345.

According to the Aviationist, the Air Force plans to acquire 15 M-346s for its aerobatic team. Ten will be assigned to the main formation, one to the commander and four will be spares.  Another five will join the 18 already used for training by the 61st Wing and the International Flight Training School.

The M-346’s performance differs from that of the MB-339, so the team will need to adapt its display routine. With deliveries expected to begin in 2027, the first full display season on the new jet is currently pencilled in for 2028.

The M-346’s technical credentials

Leonardo, which manufactured the aircraft, describes the M-346 as “the backbone” of the International Flight Training School in Decimomannu in Sardinia.

The advanced flight training centre is used by military pilots from Air Forces around the world and was created through collaboration between the manufacturer itself and the Italian Air Force.

The jet is optimised for advanced military pilot training, offering a broad range of training capabilities and long-term reliability, according to Leonardo. It features a wingspan of 31.9 ft, and a maximum speed of 1,090km/h.

The twin-engine, tandem-seat aircraft is equipped with a fly-by-wire flight control system with quadruple redundancy. With its Auxiliary Power Unit (APU), it can also be operated in complete autonomy.

The type has a long track record. The first prototype flew in July 2004 and Leonardo says the M-346 has already logged more than 125,000 flight hours with 126 sold worldwide.

The post Air New Zealand welcomes first Boeing 787 in seven years as economy sleeping pods delayed appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Air New Zealand has received its first new Boeing 787-9 in seven years, featuring the world's first certified iMTOW capability.
  • The higher-weight Dreamliner boosts flexibility on ultra-long-haul routes, allowing more passengers, baggage and cargo to be carried.
  • Skynest economy sleeping pods have been delayed by certification approvals, pushing their debut beyond the summer peak season.

Air New Zealand has welcomed its first new Boeing 787 Dreamliner in seven years, with the aircraft arriving in Auckland on 29 October.

The Boeing 787-9, registered ZK-NZT, is the world’s first certified Dreamliner featuring increased maximum take-off weight capability, allowing greater flexibility to carry passengers, baggage and cargo on long-haul routes.

However, the airline has confirmed that its much-anticipated Skynest economy sleeping pods will not be introduced in December as planned. It says “regulatory certification is taking longer than anticipated”, and has pushed back the launch into next year.

Air New Zealand receives first higher-weight Boeing 787 Dreamliner

The new aircraft arrived in Auckland from San Antonio, Texas, marking Air New Zealand’s first new Dreamliner delivery since 2019.

Its increased maximum take-off weight capability is designed to provide additional flexibility on ultra-long-haul flights, particularly Air New Zealand’s nonstop Auckland–New York service.

Air New Zealand became the launch customer for the Boeing 787-9 in 2014 and has since made the type a central part of its long-haul fleet. A second new Dreamliner, registered ZK-NZS, is expected to arrive within days.

The newly delivered aircraft features Air New Zealand’s latest cabin interiors, with 219 seats comprising eight Business Premier Luxe, 34 Business Premier, 52 Premium Economy and 125 Economy seats.

The Economy cabin includes nine Skycouch seats and 24 Economy Stretch seats. Air New Zealand Chief Customer and Digital Officer Jeremy O’Brien said: “There’s something really special about welcoming a brand-new aircraft into the fleet, particularly one that’s been years in the making to design, test and refine with our customers. Now we’re getting to see all that work come to life.”

What are Air New Zealand’s Skynest economy sleeping pods?

First unveiled in 2020, Skynest is designed to offer Economy and Premium Economy passengers a lie-flat sleeping experience without upgrading to Business Class.

Skynest is a six-pod sleep zone arranged in a triple-tier bunk configuration, positioned between economy and premium economy cabins.

It is a radical rethink of how long-haul economy comfort is sold and experienced. Passengers will still sit in their economy seat, but they can book a four-hour sleep session in a dedicated bunk-style pod between meal services.

Each pod measures approximately 2.03 metres in length and includes a mattress, seatbelt and privacy curtain.

The pods are intended for selected ultra-long-haul flights, including services between Auckland and New York.

Skynest was initially expected to enter service in 2024, but its introduction was postponed following delays in the delivery of Air New Zealand’s new Dreamliners.

As Air New Zealand brings back berths on planes, here’s what to expect from its new economy Skynest As Air New Zealand brings back berths on planes, here’s what to expect from its new economy Skynest

Why have Air New Zealand’s Skynest sleeping pods been delayed?

The airline had planned to introduce its Skynest sleeping pods in December 2026, giving Economy and Premium Economy passengers the opportunity to lie flat during ultra-long-haul flights.

However, Air New Zealand has confirmed that two regulatory approvals remain outstanding.

According to the airline, an overseas certifying authority has been unable to complete its approval within the original timeframe because of resource constraints. A separate certification process involving a local regulator is progressing well.

Rather than delay the introduction of its new Dreamliners, Air New Zealand has decided to put the aircraft into service during the busy summer travel period and install Skynest afterwards.

O’Brien said: “We’ve got a fantastic new 787 Dreamliner ready to welcome customers, and with summer being our busiest time of year, we want it in the air doing what it was built to do.”

He added: “Rather than hold back a brand-new aircraft while the final approvals are completed, we’ve decided to get it flying and bring Skynest onboard after the summer peak.

“We’ll confirm the new launch date for the Skynest once the timeline is clear.”

Air New Zealand continues Boeing 787 cabin upgrades

While Skynest remains delayed, Air New Zealand is continuing its wider programme of long-haul cabin improvements.

The majority of the airline’s existing Boeing 787-9 aircraft have already received refurbished interiors, with the final upgraded aircraft expected to return to service before the end of 2026.

The programme includes new Business Premier Luxe seats alongside redesigned Business Premier, Premium Economy and Economy cabins.

Air New Zealand also plans to introduce new Business Premier and Economy cabins across its Boeing 777 fleet during 2027.

]]> NASA astronauts complete 100th US ISS spacewalk: Here’s how spacewalks work https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/100th-us-spacewalk-iss-solar-array-installation/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:09:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55020 The landmark mission installed a new solar array, increased the station's power-generating capacity and highlighted the complex work astronauts carry out beyond the safety of the ISS.

The post NASA astronauts complete 100th US ISS spacewalk: Here’s how spacewalks work appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 7 min read
  • NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed the 100th US spacewalk from the International Space Station.
  • The astronauts installed and deployed the ISS's seventh roll-out solar array, part of a programme to boost the station's power supply by up to 30%.
  • The mission also offers a closer look at how astronauts train for, prepare for and carry out spacewalks in the vacuum of space.

Two astronauts have completed a seven-hour spacewalk outside the International Space Station (ISS), installing and deploying a new solar array in a mission that marked the 100th US spacewalk from the orbiting laboratory.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent seven hours and 11 minutes working outside the station on 29 October. They returned to the Quest airlock at 3:08 p.m. Eastern Time after successfully installing the seventh of eight planned roll-out solar arrays.

Although it was the 100th US spacewalk conducted from the ISS without a visiting space shuttle docked to it, the mission was the 285th spacewalk overall in support of the station. The larger figure includes 66 spacewalks from the Russian segment and 119 carried out by visiting space shuttle crews.

The new equipment will help provide electricity for the station’s experiments, life-support systems and other operations. NASA says the additional power will also support the ISS’s eventual safe and controlled return to Earth.

The spacewalk was Menon’s fourth but Kutryk’s first. It was also the first by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured outside the station with NASA astronaut Anne McClain.

A seven-hour job outside the space station

Menon and Kutryk began their spacewalk at 7:57 a.m. Eastern Time, leaving the station through its Quest airlock.

Menon wore a spacesuit marked with red stripes, while Kutryk wore an unmarked white suit, allowing mission controllers and television viewers to distinguish between them.

Their principal task was to install an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, known as an IROSA, on the station’s 2A electrical power channel.

The equipment had been delivered earlier in October aboard a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft. It was temporarily stored on a platform outside the ISS until the astronauts could install it.

The solar array weighs approximately 340 kg and measures about three metres long in its packed configuration.

After releasing it from its temporary mounting, Menon attached himself to the end of Canadarm2, the station’s Canadian-built robotic arm. Carrying the folded solar array, he travelled on the arm towards the installation site on the station’s port-side structure.

Kutryk made his way separately along the station’s framework, remaining secured by safety tethers.

Once together at the worksite, the astronauts mounted the equipment and connected it to the station’s electrical system.

Unlike conventional solar panels that require motors to unfold, the new array uses stored energy in flexible carbon-composite supports to unroll itself.

The panel extended to approximately 19 metres in length. It took about just over 11 minutes to deploy fully.

The astronauts also completed additional preparatory work for the next spacewalk, including tasks involving the mounting equipment for the eighth and final roll-out array.

Why the space station needs more electricity

The ISS has relied on large solar panels to generate electricity since its assembly began in orbit.

But the original arrays have exceeded their intended 15-year service life, and their power output has declined with age.

NASA has been adding smaller, more efficient roll-out arrays alongside the older panels rather than replacing the entire original system.

The new panels partly cover the existing arrays while generating additional electricity.

When all eight roll-out arrays are installed, NASA expects the station’s available power to increase by up to 30%, raising its generating capacity from approximately 160 kilowatts to 215 kilowatts.

The extra electricity will support scientific research, station equipment and essential operations during the remaining years of the ISS programme.

It will also help maintain the systems needed for the station’s planned controlled deorbit at the end of its operational life.

Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to conduct another spacewalk on 5 November to install the eighth and final roll-out array on the 3B electrical power channel.

That installation is expected to complete the station’s solar power upgrade programme.

How the astronauts prepared for the spacewalk

The work outside the ISS was the result of several days of preparation by the station’s Expedition 75 crew.

Earlier in the week, Menon and Kutryk rehearsed the movements needed to carry the solar array from its storage platform to the installation site.

Their colleagues, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, practised operating Canadarm2 and reviewed the camera positions and lighting conditions needed to monitor the work.

The two spacewalkers organised their tools inside the Quest airlock and prepared small checklists that could be attached to the cuffs of their spacesuits.

They also checked their suits’ oxygen, cooling, water and communications systems. Their emergency jetpacks were inspected to ensure that the batteries, fuel supplies and thrusters were working.

On Wednesday, the four astronauts held final discussions with specialists on Earth, reviewing the installation procedure and the robotic arm’s movements.

Watkins and Delaney remained inside the station during Thursday’s operation, helping the spacewalkers prepare and supporting the work outside.

What is a spacewalk and how is it done?

A spacewalk is any activity in which an astronaut leaves a spacecraft while in space. NASA calls it an extravehicular activity, or EVA.

Despite the name, astronauts do not actually walk. In the absence of normal gravity, they move by holding onto handrails, pulling themselves along structures or using equipment such as robotic arms.

Spacewalks allow astronauts to repair equipment, install new hardware and carry out experiments that cannot be performed inside a spacecraft.

Before leaving the station, astronauts put on specially designed spacesuits that function much like miniature spacecraft. They provide oxygen for breathing, regulate body temperature, maintain pressure and allow communication with the crew and mission controllers.

Preparation begins several hours before the astronauts go outside.

One important precaution is breathing pure oxygen to remove excess nitrogen from the body. Without this procedure, changes in pressure could cause nitrogen bubbles to form in the bloodstream and tissues, producing a painful condition known as decompression sickness, or the bends. Scuba divers face a similar risk.

Astronauts leave through an airlock, a small chamber with two doors. The inner door is closed before air is removed from the chamber, allowing the outer hatch to open without releasing the station’s atmosphere into space.

Once outside, astronauts remain attached to the station by safety tethers. Their tools are also secured to prevent them from floating away.

They carry an emergency device called SAFER, short for Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue. Worn like a backpack, it uses small thrusters that an astronaut can control with a hand-operated device to return to the station if accidentally separated from it.

A typical ISS spacewalk lasts between five and eight hours, depending on the work involved.

Training for work in the vacuum of space

Long before astronauts attempt these operations in orbit, they practise on Earth.

One of NASA’s main training facilities is the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory near Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

The enormous swimming pool contains approximately 6.2 million gallons of water and allows astronauts wearing training spacesuits to rehearse tasks around submerged replicas of spacecraft structures.

By carefully adjusting their buoyancy, instructors can recreate some of the difficulties of moving and handling equipment in weightlessness.

Astronauts also use virtual reality systems to practise working outside the station. Special headsets and gloves allow them to rehearse movements, become familiar with their surroundings and prepare for complicated operations.

These rehearsals are especially important because even simple tasks can become difficult in bulky, pressurised spacesuits.

From the first spacewalk in 1965 to the ISS’s 100th US excursion

The history of spacewalking began more than six decades ago.

On 18 March 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov became the first person to leave a spacecraft in orbit. His historic spacewalk lasted about ten minutes.

Less than three months later, on 3 June 1965, NASA astronaut Ed White became the first American to conduct a spacewalk during the Gemini 4 mission. He spent approximately 23 minutes outside his spacecraft.

Spacewalking later became essential to human space exploration, particularly during the construction of the ISS.

Astronauts helped assemble the station in orbit, connecting modules, installing equipment and carrying out repairs that could not be completed by robots alone.

The first US spacewalk from the station’s Quest airlock took place on 20 February 2002, when NASA astronauts Carl Walz and Daniel Bursch spent five hours and 47 minutes testing its systems and carrying out maintenance.

The record for the most spacewalks by an individual astronaut belongs to Russian cosmonaut Anatoly Solovyev, who completed 16 excursions totalling more than 82 hours.

]]> NASA’s ‘quiet Son of Concorde’ vs the original: Is the X-59 faster? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/nasa-x59-vs-concorde-speed-sonic-boom/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 13:11:03 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55022 As NASA advances testing of the X-59, comparisons with Concorde are inevitable. Here's how the two supersonic aircraft stack up.

The post NASA’s ‘quiet Son of Concorde’ vs the original: Is the X-59 faster? appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • NASA's X-59 is designed to make supersonic flight quieter for people on the ground.
  • The aircraft is testing technologies that could influence future aviation regulations.
  • Comparisons with Concorde highlight how supersonic ambitions have evolved over time.

At first glance, NASA‘s X-59 Quesst looks like a modern-day Concorde. Yet the experimental aircraft has been designed with a completely different objective in mind.

Here’s how NASA’s X-59 compares with Concorde across speed, altitude, design and supersonic noise.

X-59 vs Concorde: Which aircraft is faster?

The X-59 has reached Mach 1.53 during flight testing, faster than its planned cruising speed of Mach 1.4. But it still has some way to go to match Concorde.

The iconic Anglo-French airliner cruised at Mach 2.04, approximately 1,354 mph (2,179 km/h), carrying 100 passengers between Europe and the United States in around three and a half hours.

The X-59, developed by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works for NASA, has reached approximately 1,010 mph (1,625 km/h). Its usual operating speed will be around 925 mph (1,490 km/h).

Why sonic booms happen and how NASA’s X-59 Quesst plans to eliminate them Why sonic booms happen and how NASA’s X-59 Quesst plans to eliminate them

How do Concorde and the X-59 compare?

Concorde entered commercial service in 1976 with British Airways and Air France and retired in 2003. It remains the fastest passenger aircraft ever to have flown. 

The X-59, which first flew in October 2025, is an experimental aircraft with room for just one pilot.

Why was Concorde restricted in the United States?

Concorde’s sonic boom was loud enough to disturb people on the ground, which hampered supersonic operations.

The US Federal Aviation Administration introduced restrictions on civilian supersonic flights over land in 1973. Concorde could fly to New York JFK and Washington Dulles, but had to slow below the speed of sound when operating over US territory.

That kept airlines from taking advantage of its full performance on domestic transcontinental routes, limiting Concorde’s commercial appeal.

The X-59’s design prevents shockwaves from combining into the loud boom that Concorde produced. Its long, narrow nose separates the pressure waves generated at the front of the aircraft from those produced by the wings. NASA has also kept the underside of the aircraft smooth and mounted its engine above the fuselage, where the wings help shield the ground from the engine inlet’s shockwaves. 

The space agency expects people on the ground will only hear a quiet thump, more like a car door closing from about 20 feet away.

The noise-dampening design presents a challenge for piloting the aircraft. The X-59’s nose is so long that its pilot cannot see directly forward through a windscreen. Instead, pilots rely on camera images shown on a cockpit display to see what’s ahead.

NASA’s X-59 has already exceeded its target speed

The aircraft first broke the sound barrier on 5 June 2026, reaching approximately Mach 1.1.

A week later, on 12 June, it reached Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet, the conditions NASA has planned for its future noise research flights.

During testing in September, NASA pushed the X-59 to Mach 1.53, its highest reported speed. By the first anniversary of its maiden flight on 28 October, it had completed 40 additional flights and reached altitudes above 56,000 feet.

NASA is now preparing for acoustic testing to measure the aircraft’s actual noise levels. Flights over selected US communities will follow, allowing researchers to record how residents respond.

NASA hopes the findings will give regulators the evidence they need to establish noise limits for future supersonic passenger aircraft. The FAA is already working to replace the longstanding US restrictions with noise-based standards, with rulemaking milestones planned for 2027.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Royal Navy F-35Bs from HMS Prince of Wales joined Norwegian F-35As to escort a USAF B-52 over the High North.
  • The sortie supported Global Thunder 27, USSTRATCOM’s annual strategic deterrence and nuclear command-and-control exercise.
  • The mission highlighted NATO integration between carrier-based fighters, land-based F-35s and US long-range bomber operations.

For the first time, British F-35B stealth fighters have escorted a US B-52 bomber in the High North

The F-35Bs took off from HMS Prince of Wales and were joined in the escort by Norwegian F-35As flying from the mainland.

Norwegian and British F-35s escort US B-52 in exercise

The Royal Navy’s HMS Prince of Wales, accompanied by HMS Dauntless, is currently taking part in Operation Firecrest as part of Neptune Strike 26-4. The group has been joined by Norway’s HNoMS Fridtjof Nansen.

On the 24th of October, the British F-35Bs from the embarked 617 Squadron joined Norwegian F-35As in escorting a US Air Force B-52. An RAF Voyager tanker (Airbus A330 MRTT) also took part.

Images released show the bomber flanked by six F-35 fighter jets with three on each side in close formation.

A second B-52 had been expected to take part (callsign HUSH 12), but it suffered a technical issue and did not make it, according to the media reports. The lone B-52 took off from Minot Air Base in North Dakota with the callsign HUSH 11 and was refuelled by multiple aerial refuelling tankers en-route.

Phase two of Operation Firecrest

Operation Firecrest is the second phase of the 2026 UK Carrier Strike Group deployment to the High North and involves Norwegian, Danish, and German forces.

The Royal Navy has repeatedly mentioned Operation Firecrest and other multinational efforts in the High North in the context of increased Russian aggression in the region and safeguarding strategic infrastructure such as sub-sea cables.

The British carrier strike group posted, “For the first time, an American B-52 was escorted by British F-35s, whilst working alongside Norwegian F-35s. A milestone for the UK, USA and Norway, and another example of what can be achieved when allies work as one.”

The Royal Navy stated the carrier strike group demonstrated the “operational effectiveness of Carrier Strike, launching UK F-35s, to escort a US B-52 along with Norwegian F-35s…”

Norway is notable for being the first country to officially complete its F-35 programme of record, having received all of its 52 planned fighter jets. It has divested of its legacy F-16 fighter jets to Romania and Ukraine.

UK criticized for sending F-35s to the Middle East without enough spare parts UK criticized for sending F-35s to the Middle East without enough spare parts

The US’s Global Thunder 27

Global Thunder exercises are large-scale training programmes that see US strategic forces and supporting units, alongside invited allied forces, simulate the build-up to and execution of a nuclear war scenario.

USSTRATCOM announced US Strategic Command began its annual Global Thunder nuclear command and control exercise on 22nd of October. USSTRATCOM states its purpose is to “enhance nuclear readiness and ensure a safe, secure, effective and credible strategic deterrent force.”

The US stated that the exercise is not in response to actions by any nation or current world events. The exercise can see an increase in bomber and other aircraft flights.

USSTRATCOM posted that the joint operation with British and Norwegian forces visibly demonstrated a “shared commitment to global security and stability.”

An official NATO statement noted it demonstrated the ability of British, US, and Norwegian forces to “integrate strategic airpower with advanced fighter capability across the High North.”

]]> IATA survey finds visa and immigration requirements discourage 43% of travellers https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/iata-2026-passenger-survey-immigration-biometrics-ai/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 11:17:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54986 Passengers are increasingly embracing digital travel tools, with growing use of biometrics, digital identity and AI, while airlines and governments face pressure to simplify border and visa processes.

The post IATA survey finds visa and immigration requirements discourage 43% of travellers appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • IATA's 2026 Global Passenger Survey found that 43% of travellers were deterred by visa and immigration requirements, up from 33% in 2025.
  • Biometric airport processing continues to grow, with 58% of passengers using biometrics and 84% interested in digital passports.
  • AI travel planning is going mainstream, with 49% of travellers using AI to search flights, find cheaper fares and discover destinations.

Immigration requirements are discouraging many from international travel, even as passengers become more comfortable using artificial intelligence (AI), biometrics and digital passports, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA).

The findings come from an IATA survey of more than 10,000 respondents across over 200 countries, published on 28 October.

Immigration requirements dampen international travel demand 

According to IATA’s 2026 Global Passenger Survey, 43% of respondents said immigration requirements had discouraged them from visiting a destination, compared with 33% in 2025.

Among those deterred by entry requirements, 53% said the complexity of the process was their main concern. Privacy and cost were each cited by 17% of those surveyed.

IATA said governments need to simplify visa and immigration procedures to remove barriers to travel.

“Passengers are embracing technology to make travel easier. AI is becoming a mainstream travel planning tool, while biometrics and digital identity are creating a faster and more seamless airport experience. Yet many travellers continue to face barriers from complex immigration and visa processes,” said Nick Careen, IATA’s Senior Vice President, Operations, Safety and Security.

Passengers want simpler digital immigration procedures

Despite concerns about entry requirements, passengers are increasingly willing to complete immigration formalities digitally before travelling.

The survey found that 86% would be willing to share immigration information electronically before departure to speed up the process, compared with 83% in 2025.

Meanwhile, 45% would prefer to complete immigration procedures before reaching the airport, up from 41% last year.

A clear majority of travellers prefer online visa applications, with around 60% favouring applying online, compared with 25% who would rather visit an embassy or consulate.

IATA said more than 100 countries already issue electronic visas. However, differences in how these digital documents are verified create difficulties for airlines checking passenger documentation.

The association is calling for common standards that would allow airlines and governments to verify digital travel credentials more efficiently.

Biometric identification gains ground at airports

Biometric technology has become a more familiar part of the airport experience.

Some 58% of passengers reported using biometric identification during an airport journey in the previous 12 months, up from 50% in 2025 and 34% in 2022.

Among passengers who had experienced biometric processing, 87% said they were satisfied with it.

The survey also found that 78% would be willing to share biometric information to avoid repeatedly presenting a passport or boarding pass at airport checkpoints.

Interest in digital passports is particularly strong, with 84% of respondents saying they would like to use one for online check-in instead of a physical document.

However, passengers remain concerned about how their personal information is protected.

Data breaches were the leading concern, cited by 59% of respondents, followed by information being shared with other organisations (49%) and uncertainty about how personal data is handled (41%).

Nearly half of passengers use AI to plan travel

AI is also becoming part of how passengers research and arrange their journeys. The IATA survey found that 49% of respondents had used AI for travel planning. 

  • Searching for flights to a particular destination was the most common application, cited by 21% of respondents.
  • 19% used AI to find cheaper flights
  • 17% used AI to identify potential destinations.

IATA said airlines need to consider how their products appear in AI-powered searches and how passengers can move from researching a journey to making a booking.

Europe trails other regions in AI and biometric adoption

The survey revealed considerable differences in passengers’ attitudes towards digital travel technology.

Europe recorded the lowest use of AI for travel planning, at 35%, compared with the global average of 49%. Only 47% of European respondents had experienced biometric identification in the previous year, against 58% globally.

European passengers were also less willing to share biometric data, with 70% supporting its use for airport processes compared with 78% worldwide.

The Middle East recorded the highest AI adoption, at 72%, and the strongest interest in digital passports for online check-in, at 91%.

North America had the highest proportion of passengers who had experienced biometric processing, at 63%, although respondents there also expressed the greatest concern about data breaches.

Africa recorded the highest proportion of passengers discouraged by immigration requirements, at 52%, followed by Asia-Pacific at 49%. Europe’s figure was 38%, and North America had the lowest share, at 35%.

Overall, 87% of respondents said they were satisfied with air travel, although satisfaction in Europe was the lowest of any region, at 84%.

IATA’s 2026 Global Passenger Survey shows clear progress in many parts of the digital journey, but government policy still requires harmonisation before truly seamless travel becomes a reality.

]]> Archer Aviation and ITA Airways plan electric air taxi services in Italy https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/archer-ita-airways-electric-air-taxis-italy/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 10:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54970 Archer Aviation and ITA Airways have agreed to explore an electric air taxi network in Italy using the Midnight eVTOL aircraft for faster airport-to-city connections.

The post Archer Aviation and ITA Airways plan electric air taxi services in Italy appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Archer and ITA Airways are exploring electric air taxi services in Italy, using Archer's Midnight eVTOL aircraft.
  • Rome airport-to-city connections are a key target, with flights intended to cut travel times compared with road journeys.
  • Commercial flights are still some way off, with approvals and infrastructure needed before the service can launch.

Archer Aviation and ITA Airways have signed an agreement to partner on an electric air taxi network in Italy, which could connect major airports with city centres using Archer’s Midnight aircraft.

The Lufthansa Group airline is the first European carrier to join Archer’s international network of airline partners.

The companies will explore opportunities to introduce electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) services in major Italian cities, with Rome among the potential locations.

Archer says its Midnight aircraft could shorten journeys that currently take 60 to 90 minutes by road to flights lasting between 10 and 20 minutes.

One proposed application is a connection between Rome Fiumicino Airport and the city centre. According to Archer, the journey could take less than 10 minutes by air, compared with approximately an hour by car.

ITA Airways explores airport-to-city air taxi connections

ITA Airways will help develop the network by coordinating with aviation and transport stakeholders and exploring how air taxi services could connect with its existing airline operations.

The carrier, which serves more than 70 destinations worldwide, would integrate the proposed services into the passenger journey. Specialist partners would operate the aircraft.

Joerg Eberhart, Chief Executive Officer and General Manager of ITA Airways, said the agreement would allow the airline to assess how electric aircraft could complement conventional air services.

“This agreement with Archer represents an important step in assessing how electric air taxi services could complement our network and enhance connections between airports, city centres and other strategic destinations,” he said. “As part of this process, we are exploring different solutions to identify the best possible product for our customers.”

Archer Midnight targets short urban flights

Archer’s Midnight is an electric aircraft designed for short journeys between airports and urban destinations.

The company is developing the aircraft for frequent, consecutive flights, which could provide an alternative to road transport in congested metropolitan areas.

Midnight produces no direct emissions during flight, although its overall environmental impact will depend partly on the electricity used to charge it.

Archer recently conducted several days of piloted demonstration flights in California’s San Francisco Bay Area, including flights between Oakland and San Francisco’s Marina District that took approximately 10 minutes.

Adam Goldstein, founder and CEO of Archer, pointed to Italy’s tourism market as an opportunity for the proposed service.

“Italy is one of the most visited countries on Earth: Rome Fiumicino crossed 50 million passengers last year for the first time in its history,” he said. “Every one of those travellers deserves the option to skip an hour in traffic with a 10-minute, all-electric flight.”

Archer expands airline partnerships across Europe, Asia and the US

The agreement with ITA Airways adds another airline to Archer’s international partners, which already includes United Airlines, Southwest Airlines, Japan Airlines, Korean Air and Ethiopian Airlines.

In the US, Archer has been working with United Airlines on proposed airport-to-city air taxi connections. The companies outlined plans for a New York network in April 2025, including flights between Manhattan and nearby airports that could take five to 15 minutes.

Archer also signed an agreement with Southwest Airlines in July 2024 to explore electric air taxi connections at California airports.

In Asia, Korean Air agreed to become Archer’s exclusive partner in South Korea in October 2025. The agreement includes a potential purchase of up to 100 Midnight aircraft, initially targeting government applications before wider commercial deployment.

Archer is also working with Japan Airlines and Sumitomo Corporation’s joint venture, Soracle, on proposed air taxi services in Japan. The partnership has been selected to participate in projects in Tokyo and Osaka.

In Africa, Ethiopian Airlines signed an agreement in March 2025 to introduce Midnight aircraft under Archer’s Launch Edition programme.

Abu Dhabi Aviation was Archer’s first announced customer.

The ITA Airways partnership gives Archer another potential European market, although the proposed services will depend on obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals, finalising operating arrangements and building supporting infrastructure.

]]> Four killed as Italian CH-47 Chinook crashes in Bosnia https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/italian-chinook-crashes-bosnia/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:02:13 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54962 Four people were killed when an Italian Army CH-47 Chinook crashed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, putting the spotlight on one of the world's most widely operated military helicopters.

The post Four killed as Italian CH-47 Chinook crashes in Bosnia appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 2 min read
  • An Italian Army CH-47 Chinook crashed during a training flight in Bosnia and Herzegovina, killing four people and injuring 11 others.
  • The helicopter was supporting the EU's Operation Althea peacekeeping mission when it came down near Gorice in the Brčko district.
  • Investigators are working to determine the cause, while the crash has put the spotlight on one of the world's most widely used military helicopters.

An Italian Army CH-47 Chinook operating with the EU peacekeeping mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina has crashed during a training flight, killing four people and injuring 11 others.

The accident occurred near Gorice in the Brčko district and has renewed attention on military helicopter safety as investigators work to establish the cause.

Italian CH-47 Chinook helicopter crashes in Bosnia with 15 onboard

According to Italy’s defence ministry, four were killed, and 11 were injured, none of whom had life-threatening injuries.

Two of those dead were members of the Italian army, and two were part of the Italian Red Cross’ Volunteer Military Corps.

Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto stated, “At this moment ​of immense grief, my thoughts go first and foremost to the families ​of our fallen, to whom I extend my personal condolences and those of the entire Defence establishment.”

Unverified video shared on social media appeared to capture the final moments of the flight.

The helicopter had been deployed as part of Operation Althea, a mission run by the European Union Force (EUFOR) that oversees the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement.

The Associated Press states that EUFOR’s 1,200-soldier mission took over from NATO in 2004 to help maintain security and oversee the military provisions of a peace agreement that ended the 1992–95 war.

EUFOR appeals to avoid misinformation about the crash

EUFOR reported it will conduct a “thorough and complete investigation to ascertain the facts which led to this tragic accident.” It will release details as they become available and verified.

In its statement, EUFOR appealed for all to avoid misinformation regarding the incident and “to refrain from any speculation regarding the nationalities and identities of EUFOR personnel involved, and to refer only to official EUFOR channels for verified updates.”

It warns that spreading unverified claims on the identities and nationalities of those involved, along with the circumstances, may lead to “unnecessary public concern.”

Boeing begins production of first of 60 CH-47F Block II helicopters for Germany Boeing begins production of first of 60 CH-47F Block II helicopters for Germany

The safety record of the CH-47 Chinook

The CH-47 Chinook is among the world’s most widely operated military helicopters. First entering service in the early 1960s, the twin-rotor aircraft is used by armed forces around the world for heavy-lift transport, troop movements and humanitarian support missions.

More than 1,200 Chinooks have been built, with the type remaining in frontline service across Europe, North America, Asia and the Middle East.

According to Aviation Safety Network data, 61 CH-47 helicopters have been written off worldwide since 2000, including aircraft lost during military operations. Six of those write-offs have occurred since 2020.

In the US Army, the largest operator of the type, Chinooks flew more than 386,000 flight hours between 2019 and 2020, according to Army safety data. Over that period, the fleet recorded six Class A mishaps, seven Class B mishaps and 34 Class C mishaps.

]]> IndiGo launches world’s longest Airbus A321XLR flight with 11-hour Amsterdam route https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/indigo-worlds-longest-airbus-a321xlr-flight/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 06:31:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54865 IndiGo has launched the world's longest scheduled Airbus A321XLR flight between Mumbai and Amsterdam. Here's how it compares to other long A321XLR routes.

The post IndiGo launches world’s longest Airbus A321XLR flight with 11-hour Amsterdam route appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • IndiGo’s 11-hour Mumbai–Amsterdam service is the world’s longest scheduled A321XLR route, replacing a leased Boeing 787-9.
  • The airline reportedly sells fewer than 140 of its 195 seats on Amsterdam-bound flights to accommodate fuel requirements and longer routings.
  • American Airlines’ planned Philadelphia–Vienna service could take the distance record in May 2027, although IndiGo’s flight has a longer scheduled duration.

IndiGo has begun operating the world’s longest scheduled Airbus A321XLR flight, using the single-aisle aircraft on its 11-hour service between Mumbai and Amsterdam.

The Indian airline introduced the A321XLR on 25 October 2026, replacing the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner previously operated under a lease agreement with Norse Atlantic Airways.

At approximately 3,707 nautical miles (6,865 km), Mumbai–Amsterdam is the longest A321XLR route, as confirmed by Cirium’s October 2026 schedule data. It also has one of the longest scheduled flight times for a single-aisle passenger aircraft.

As AGN reported earlier this week, IndiGo’s move away from leased Dreamliners has reduced its available capacity on European routes. The change lets IndiGo continue its Amsterdam service while awaiting deliveries of its own Airbus A350-900 widebodies, expected from 2028.

The airline is reportedly restricting passenger numbers to make the long journey possible. According to Aviacionline, IndiGo is offering fewer than 140 seats on the Amsterdam-bound flight, despite the aircraft having 195 seats installed. That leaves at least 55 seats, approximately 28% of the cabin, unsold.

Why IndiGo’s 11-hour Amsterdam flight needs empty seats

IndiGo’s Mumbai–Amsterdam flight, 6E21, has a scheduled block time of 11 hours and five minutes. The return service, 6E22, takes nine hours and 40 minutes.

The great-circle distance between Mumbai and Amsterdam is approximately 3,707 nautical miles. But airspace restrictions are forcing the aircraft to fly a longer route through the Middle East. The actual distance flown can approach 4,200 nautical miles, depending on the routing.

Airbus advertises a maximum range of 4,700 nautical miles for the A321XLR, but that does not mean airlines can carry a full passenger load over that distance.

Range depends on aircraft weight, fuel reserves, weather conditions, and the route flown. Westbound headwinds can also increase fuel consumption.

IndiGo’s A321XLR has 12 IndiGo Stretch premium seats and 183 economy seats.

Limiting passenger numbers reduces the aircraft’s payload, helping it remain within operating weight limits while carrying sufficient fuel for the journey.

Despite the capacity restrictions, IndiGo has maintained daily Mumbai–Amsterdam operations.

The airline first planned to reduce the service to three weekly flights after replacing the Boeing 787. However, it later restored daily frequencies from October through late January.

The airline’s latest schedule filing on Aeroroutes shows flights reduced to three weekly from 20 January 2027, operating on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays until late March.

What are the world’s longest Airbus A321XLR routes?

IndiGo has overtaken Iberia‘s Madrid–Santo Domingo service, previously one of the longest scheduled A321XLR operations.

The Spanish airline was the launch operator of the A321XLR in November 2024 and has since expanded its use across the Atlantic.

In an October 2026 analysis, Cirium reported that Iberia had operated more than 400 A321XLR flights exceeding 5,000 km by July.

Other airlines, including Aer Lingus and American Airlines, have introduced the aircraft on transatlantic services.

The 10 longest A321XLR routes

The following table compares ten of the longest identified A321XLR routes, taken from an October 2026–March 2027 Cirium schedule extract.

Rank* Airline Route Distance (nm)
1IndiGoMumbai–Amsterdam3,707
2IberiaMadrid–Santo Domingo3,617
3IberiaMadrid–San Juan3,449
4Aer LingusDublin–Nashville3,394
5IberiaMadrid–Recife3,386
6American AirlinesNew York JFK–Barcelona3,329
7IberiaMadrid–Washington Dulles3,317
8IberiaMadrid–Toronto3,280
9IberiaMadrid–Fortaleza3,271
10Aer LingusDublin–Indianapolis3,230
 *Selected A321XLR routes identified in Cirium’s October 2026–March 2027 schedules, ranked by approximate great-circle distance. Source: Cirium Diio; airline schedules.

The ranking excludes Aer Lingus’ seasonal Dublin–Bridgetown XLR service, which operated earlier in 2026 but is not part of the current winter schedule comparison.

Iberia features prominently, with long XLR services to Santo Domingo, San Juan, Recife and Fortaleza. The airline has also increased frequencies to its Brazilian destinations.

According to AeroRoutes, Iberia plans up to 11 weekly A321XLR flights between Madrid and Recife and 10 weekly flights to Fortaleza during parts of December 2026 and January 2027.

American Airlines is also expanding its A321XLR network. Cirium identifies New York JFK–Barcelona among the airline’s XLR deployments beginning in October 2026.

Unlike IndiGo, which is using the XLR to maintain an existing long-haul route previously served by a widebody, American and Iberia have deployed the narrowbody aircraft to serve markets where larger jets may be harder to fill profitably.

More airlines plan long A321XLR flights in 2027

IndiGo’s lead in the distance ranking may not last. American Airlines also plans to introduce the A321XLR between Philadelphia and Vienna in May 2027.

At approximately 3,755 nautical miles, the route would exceed Mumbai–Amsterdam’s great-circle distance. However, its published block time of around 10 hours and 15 minutes remains shorter than IndiGo’s 11-hour service.

Air Canada plans to introduce the A321XLR between Toronto and Copenhagen in November 2026, replacing a Boeing 787-8 on selected flights. At approximately 3,390 nautical miles, the route would rank among the longest XLR services, although it is shorter than Mumbai–Amsterdam.

While the aircraft is opening up new, long routes, it still has narrowbody limitations.

IndiGo’s Amsterdam service shows that even an aircraft designed for exceptionally long narrowbody flights may need to sacrifice some passenger bookings when routing and fuel requirements push it towards its operating limits.

 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}

 left: 0;
 right: 0;

.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

<div class="lc-padding-top-half lc-padding-bottom-default lc-background-color-white lc-contained eac-stripe eac-stripe--bg-white" id="paragraph-827">  <div class="eac-stripe__inner">            <div class="full-html-body">
  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
	<li><a class="external-link eac-external-link" href="https://twitter.com/search?q=%23TheFutureIsYours" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">#TheFutureIsYours</a></li>

</ul>
